title: Australians taking unnecessary vitamins during pregnancy, experts say
text:
Do this, take this, buy that: Social media is a minefield of misinformation for expectant parents.

And health experts say they're increasingly concerned about influencers spruiking prenatal multivitamins and promoting unnecessary supplements on their social media platforms.

Shelley Wilkinson, a prenatal dietitian and an obstetric medicine researcher at the University of Queensland, said many pregnant people were taking unnecessary supplements or multivitamins as a "top-up" or "just in case".

Dr Wilkinson said not only was this a waste of money for consumers, but taking a mix of different supplements had the potential to cause harm.

"Women will take it thinking that more is always better, but that's not the case," she said.

"It's a billion-dollar industry preying on people's vulnerabilities."

Guidelines recommend pregnant people take folic acid, iodine and — if appropriate — elemental iron daily. (Pexels: SHVETS production)

What supplements are recommended?

Australia's pregnancy care guidelines recommend all pregnant people take 400–600 micrograms of folic acid a day — ideally from four weeks before getting pregnant — to help prevent neural tube defects such as spina bifida.

They also recommend a daily supplement containing 150 micrograms of iodine, to help reduce the risks of still birth and preterm birth, although women with pre-existing thyroid conditions should discuss this with their doctor first.

What's in pregnancy supplements? Health experts say tighter regulations around pregnancy supplements are needed as newer brands replace folic acid with a lesser-studied alternative.

There's also a few newer draft recommendations on iron supplements in the guidelines, which have been approved by steering committees, but not officially adopted.

These recommendations suggest pregnant people take between 60–200 micrograms of elemental iron daily but if people experience side effects such as constipation or nausea their doctor may suggest a lower dose.

They also advise not to take high-dose vitamin A, C or E supplements because there is little to no benefit and they may actually harm.

Vitamin D supplements are also not routinely recommended during pregnancy.

There's also a range of other supplements, including omega-3, creatine and collagen, which are not routinely recommended during pregnancy but are advertised by social media influencers as having benefit and sold in stores.

Rod Pearce, who is a practising GP in South Australia and chair of the Immunisation Coalition, said he'd seen an increase in the number of people who were taking prenatal supplements they didn't need.

"General advice, if you've got a good, healthy diet in Australia, you tend not to need all these extra supplements and you're just making expensive urine," he said.

Prenatal multivitamin 'overuse'

Evidence from a 2023 small study shows many Australian women are overusing multivitamins while pregnant.

The study, led by Dr Wilkinson and University of the Sunshine Coast health researcher Linda Gallo, found nine-in-10 participants reported using supplements, with most choosing multivitamins.

"If people are buying these products and they and they don't work, or they're not giving any benefit, they are poorer for having spent the money," Dr Wilkinson said.

"But the other thing is, it's not necessarily better to take everything."

Taking too many vitamins could also cause harm, she added.

The recommended upper limit for vitamin B6 is 50 milligrams per day, and high doses can cause irreversible nerve damage.

Dr Wilkinson said many of her clients were accidentally exceeding this upper limit, with one woman unknowingly taking three different tables which all contained vitamin B6 and added up to 140 milligrams daily.

Shelley Wilkinson and Linda Gallo's previous research indicates women are overusing multivitamins in pregnancy. (Supplied: Shelley Wilkinson/Linda Gallo)

Dr Wilkinson said if someone did choose to use multivitamins it was also important to note that prenatal and regular multivitamins were not the same.

Multivitamins made for pregnant people don't contain vitamin A which in high doses can harm a developing baby.

But Dr Wilkinson advises ditching prenatal multivitamin altogether and take iron, folate and iodine supplements separately.

This, she said, would save people money and minimise the potential for harm.

Dr Gallo said taking prenatal multivitamins as well as additional doses of the recommended folate, iodine and iron, could lead to negative outcomes such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia and preterm birth.

Dr Gallo said, when asked, patients who had accidentally overused supplements were motivated by the desire for good pregnancy outcomes.

"The vast majority will say, 'Well, I'd just do anything I can to protect my baby,'" she said.

Probing the social media influence

Despite anecdotal reports from doctors, it's not clear how many Australian women are taking advice about prenatal vitamins from social media.

It's a knowledge gap that Athena Hooymans, PhD candidate from the University of the Sunshine Coast, is attempting to fill.

Mrs Hooymans said she was "very surprised" about the lack of evidence available about what women were taking in Australia.

ABC Health in your Instagram feed Follow @abchealth on Instagram, where we're busting myths and sharing practical, smart health advice.

She's asking people about the type of prenatal supplements they're taking and who recommended them — whether that's a doctor, a friend or a social media influencer.

Dr Gallo, who has been supervising this research, said although Australia had solid guidelines, they weren't very user friendly and most women didn't know how to find or navigate them.

After sifting through the survey results, Mrs Hooymans and Dr Gallo hope to interview participants before pulling together some educational material for doctors to use to discuss supplements and multivitamins with their patients.

Dr Gallo said some of her yet-to-be-published research showed many Australian doctors were not aware that iron was now routinely recommended, showing a slight disconnect.

Sara Whitburn, practising GP and chair of the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners' sexual and reproductive health special interest group, said the advice across a range of areas — including pregnancy care guidelines — was often being updated, and it was a lot for GPs to stay across.

She urged expectant patients who saw prenatal health information on social media to be cautious, and to consider if the person posting that information was being paid for the content and if the claims were backed by scientific evidence.

"When you're looking at social media, ask yourself: 'What resources are they using? What are their references?'" she said.

"Try and check some of these other websites that are showing the [pregnancy care] guidelines, showing evidence-based information and trying to put those together and hopefully come out with a balanced approach."

'Food first' approach recommended

As well as taking folate, iron and iodine, Dr Gallo said the best thing that pregnant women could do for their health was stay active and eat a wide variety of healthy food.

This meant limiting caffeine, avoiding alcohol and eating lots of wholefoods, a mix of different coloured fruits and vegetables as well as whole grains and iron-rich foods, Dr Gallo said.

"A very nutrient-rich diet should be absolutely the foundation," she said.

Many pregnant women are taking vitamins they don't need, experts say, instead of eating healthy diets. (Unsplash: Ksenia Yakovleva)

But Dr Gallo said evidence suggested just one-in-four pregnant women were eating the recommended serves of vegetables and legumes, prompting the need for specialists to chat about dietary needs with their pregnant patients.

Dr Wilkinson said patients should talk to their doctors about any and all supplements they took, even if they were advertised as all-natural or safe products, in case a combination could lead to a vitamin overload.

She said people with diagnosed vitamin deficiencies or complex health issues should talk to their doctor about whether they needed additional supplements, as well as iron, iodine and folate.

Everyone else, she advised taking a "food-first approach" to making sure they were getting all the vitamins they needed.

"No-one can get enough iodine and folate from diet alone," she said.

"But all the other supplements, we should be spending our time talking to women about how to include it in their diet, rather than popping these pills.

"And if you have a health question, talk to your doctor or someone who's qualified."

title: Crippling costs force family to close mushroom farm after 45 years
text:
Joanne and Steve Willemse did everything they could to keep the gates open at their commercial mushroom farm at Chevallum, on Queensland's Sunshine Coast.

They downsized their business, sold an apartment, and the investment property they had bought to fund their retirement.

"It's got to the stage now where we're not making any money at all, we're actually losing money," Ms Willemse said.

" On average, we're losing about $10,000 a week. "

Joanne Willemse holds one of the last boxes of Swiss brown mushrooms produced at the farm. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Family-owned SjW Mushrooms supplies IGA supermarkets, as well as dozens of fruit shops and markets.

Ms Willemse said while the price of a box of mushrooms had barely changed over the past 20 years, the cost of growing them had increased dramatically.

Price hikes caused by the Iran war have also fuelled their financial pain.

Steve and Joanne Willemse have made the difficult decision to leave the industry. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

Mushrooms are nutritious, low in kilojoules and high in vitamin B, minerals and antioxidants.

But Australian production has continued to drop since 2021.

The most recent figures from the Australian Horticulture Statistics Handbook for 2024/25 show mushroom production decreased by 12 per cent to 52,784 tonnes, valued at $338.3 million.

Consumers purchased 7 per cent fewer mushrooms that financial year.

Ingredients for vegan dan dan noodles including fresh noodles, Swiss brown mushrooms and Chinese broccoli. (ABC Life: Hetty McKinnon)

"[People are] not buying mushrooms because they're expensive. The fruit shops, they're struggling as well," Ms Willemse said.

"It's a vicious cycle.

"They want us to keep our prices down so that they can keep their prices down, so they can attract more customers."

The Willemse family has farmed mushrooms in Queensland since the 1950s.

The couple branched off on their own 15 years ago, taking over a farm at Woodford and expanding to Chevallum a year later.

Workers at the Chevallum farm were devastated to learn of the impeding closure. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

They once employed 65 staff, but that has dropped to 15.

"They've all been with us since day one so there's been quite a few tears and a lot of beautiful notes they've handed over," Ms Willemse said.

" Even our customers have sent us beautiful texts and emails. "

Their tough decision to close has meant their adult children, who help run the farm, have had to look for work.

"I have grandkids as well, and we were hoping that they would eventually take over, but that's not to be," Ms Willemse said.

The last of the mushrooms will be picked over the next week. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

'Less choice' for consumers

Adam Forbes, from wholesale fruit and vegetable supplier The Produce Partner, said he was "devastated" to learn of the farm's closure.

"We get up to a tonne of mushrooms through those guys weekly," Mr Forbes said.

"They were such a great local farm … it's really going to put a dent in the local market.

"It's going to push pricing up across the board.

Adam Forbes says growers are under increasing pressure and struggling to stay afloat. (Supplied: The Produce Partner)

"Chefs, restaurants, they can't push their prices up any further and so the farmers are getting the rough end of the stick."

Tough environment

AUSVEG spokesperson Andrew MacDonald said business conditions were "extremely challenging".

Vegetable costs rise Farmers kept planting through the uncertainty of the US Iran war. Now they're paying for it.

He said production costs had surged, compliance burdens were more unsustainable, and skills and workforce shortages made it challenging to secure viable returns.

"It's continued to get harder … the Middle East war has compounded pressures," he said.

Describing Australian vegetable consumption as "critically low and declining," Mr MacDonald said practical support from government and consumers was "crucial for our food security".

New industry entrants

There is still optimism for the future of fungi farming.

Martin Anfosso and his partner Elona Kovach rented an industrial shed in Coolum after their business outgrew their garage.

Every week, they grow 50 kilograms of spray-free gourmet mushrooms for chefs, cafes and retail stores.

The Coolum-based business grows nine different varieties of gourmet mushrooms. (Supplied: Fleur de Fungi)

"We're about to bump up from next week to roughly 70 kilograms … everything is sourced from Australia," Mr Anfosso said.

Mountaintop Mushrooms closes its doors The business a young couple crowdfunded to grow a head-turning array of tasty, colourful fungi in a century-old pineapple packing shed closes.

But Ms Kovach said they were keenly aware of several Sunshine Coast mushroom businesses closing in recent years.

"Being a small business, I think in any niche, is very difficult," she said.

Back at SjW Mushrooms, Ms Willemse said farmers needed support.

"We pay a lot of taxes, farmers, just like any other business. However, we're a primary producer," she said.

"We feed the country."

title: Vulnerable patients fear implications of stoma nurse shortage
text:
David Platt was unsure what his future held when he awoke from surgery with a urostomy bag.

Living in Mount Gambier, in regional South Australia, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2004, but the disease spread throughout his body, including to his bladder.

It required the removal of his bladder and the creation of a stoma, a surgical opening which helped Mr Platt pass waste into the urostomy bag.

"I looked down, I thought, 'Well, I've got this thing stuck on me, what do I do?'" Mr Platt said.

The first couple of months were difficult for Mr Platt and his wife Paula, but a stoma nurse at Mount Gambier hospital helped him understand his new life.

David Platt says having support nearby allows those with a stoma to be more independent. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I think I went up there for about four changes and in the end she said, 'Look, you've mastered it, you can actually do it yourself now,'" he said.

Mr Platt eventually came to view the urostomy bag as "just part of my body".

But reaching that understanding can take time and support.

It is why he tries to help others who are still coming to terms with their own stoma bags.

Mr Platt says the medical guidance and support which helped him is under threat by a stoma nurse shortage in Mount Gambier.

The largest SA city outside Adelaide has gone from having two full-time staff to one nurse on one day a week.

Recruitment troubles

More than 200 people in the South East region have some form of stoma and Mr Platt runs the region's stoma support group.

Urostomy bags, like Mr Platt uses, collect urine, while colostomy bags collect stool and gas when organs like the colon have been removed.

"Stoma bag" is typically used to encompass both types.

Mr Platt said while everyday maintenance, such as changing bags, was typically conducted at home, more serious emergencies required a specialist nurse.

David and Paula Platt run Mount Gambier's support group. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

"I know there's a couple of women have had to go to Adelaide because they can't get the help here," he said.

"I mean it's rough really for them to have to travel all the way, especially as they're not young, they're older people in their 80s."

Limestone Coast Local Health Network (LCLHN) chief executive Emma Poland said recruitment was underway for a specialist stoma nurse in Mount Gambier.

The two previous nurses had left the position for other opportunities.

"We acknowledge we face growing competition from intrastate, interstate and overseas for qualified professionals," Ms Poland said.

Mount Gambier hospital is the largest public health facility in regional South Australia. (ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham)

"While we continue recruitment efforts, our Nursing Education Team is providing education on wound, stoma, and continence management to staff across the Limestone Coast region."

Ms Poland said staff across the region had received training in wound, stoma and continence management and some staff had undertaken workshops in Adelaide.

"LCLHN is also engaging with nursing locum agencies to identify suitably qualified candidates to temporarily support our service," she said.

"We are committed to providing a safe and high-quality stoma and continence service to support consumers across our region."

Nurse training call

Independent Member for Mount Gambier Travis Fatchen has raised the issue in state parliament and called for a rethink of how stoma nursing is incorporated into the health system.

He said nursing degrees should look at adding stoma training to the curriculum.

"Have they reached out to any of the local nurses to see what is involved to do some further training?" he said.

Travis Fatchen says a better system of stoma care should be explored. (ABC News: Josh Brine)

"That may [create] a bit of a buffer where you've got three or four nurses that are day-to-day doing their normal role, but they can be called on if and when needed to help fill these gaps."

In South Australia, the qualification course to become a stoma nurse takes a year to complete and costs $14,000.

Mr Platt said outside of specialist nurses, stomas were a knowledge gap for some health staff.

Mount Gambier has gone from having two full-time stoma nurses to just one nurse who is only available one day a week. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

He said he helped educate a new nurse on basic stoma care during a recent hospital stay.

"She said, 'I've never seen one of them before,'" he said.

"She's a fully qualified nurse and she didn't know about stoma."

Importance of community

Helen Colliver helped lead the charge for a permanent stoma nurse in the Yorke Peninsula.

She had to travel to Adelaide for support when she first received a stoma after surgery for a perforated bowel.

Helen Colliver received a stoma after bowel surgery. (ABC North and West SA: Jenae Madden)

"Fortunately for me, I didn't have a huge amount of trouble, but you're always worried that it might smell or bulge or break all of a sudden," she said.

"It really makes you antisocial.

" You don't want to go out for fear of embarrassing yourself and everybody else. "

SA Health appointed a permanent stoma nurse for the Yorke Peninsula in 2021, when the area had about 140 residents in need.

Newspaper clippings detail a community push for a stoma support nurse in the Yorke Peninsula. (ABC North and West SA: Jenae Madden)

Ms Colliver said it made a world of difference to herself and everyone else with a stoma in the community.

"At our ostomy meetings, we talk about [how] the things we ask our stoma nurse, people would really be absolutely aghast if they could hear what we talk about, because it would be very embarrassing for them," she said.

"But it's quite common for us to talk about."

title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
text:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

title: Country drivers dig deep for man tackling 'catastrophic' pothole crisis
text:
Steve Panozzo's fluorescent paintwork is renowned across north-east Victoria.

With a shake of his spray can and a check of the traffic, he darts quickly onto a broken country road to leave his mark before another vehicle whizzes by.

Mr Panozzo is no artist, though.

Steve Panozzo leaves his mark on a regional road around two large potholes. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

He instead describes himself as just "a bloke who is utterly fed up" and worried about the state of regional roads, as he sprays thousands of potholes to make them more visible to drivers.

"I am incensed, it makes me angry," he says, watching a string of vehicles swerve to avoid a pothole on the outskirts of Wodonga.

"It's a constant cycle of recurring potholes where road crews can't deal with new potholes; they have to continue to backtrack and deal with existing potholes that have reopened."

Some of the potholes Steve Panozzo finds are ankle deep. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

Mr Panozzo started marking up road damage three years ago as he became increasingly worried about driver safety, regularly witnessing drivers cross double lines to avoid crater-like holes riddling regional roads.

After spending hundreds of dollars on paint, he launched an online fundraising page in March to help fund his paint purchases.

He has raised more than $2,700 so far from about 70 donors.

A bus approaches a pothole marked by Steve Panozzo on the Kiewa Valley Highway. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

He said some people had also left donations under his motorbike helmet while he was on the road, and other drivers had escorted him to hardware stores to pay for his paint.

He said drivers facing high living costs should not have to pay to make roads safer.

"It's catastrophic," he said.

"This is my concern: that it is inevitable that … we are going to have avoidable catastrophic accidents."

Pothole promises

More than 252,000 potholes were patched up by the Department of Transport and Planning during the 2025/26 financial year, more than 10 potholes for every kilometre of road managed by the state.

A road maintenance crew patches potholes near Wodonga. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

Roads have become a hot election topic for many residents who swerve and bump their way daily on degrading surfaces.

The Victorian government is investing more than $1 billion in road maintenance this year, while the opposition has pledged $5 billion to repair and rebuild the roads if elected.

Bandiana resident Cindy Penny said she was not sure that was even enough, as she watched the same potholes outside her home repaired repeatedly and cars continue to swerve widely to avoid them.

Cindy Penny watches drivers swerve around potholes daily. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

"It's just money down the drain because every time it rains, the holes just open up," she said.

Roads will be on her mind as she heads to the polls in November with serious worries a local family will end up dead on her doorstep.

"It's a big thing for me because I have little people in my life and I don't want to see any of these families destroyed by fatalities," Ms Penny said.

Too little, too late

The ramped-up pledges to fix roads have come too late for Albury resident Andrea Lever.

Andrea Lever has lost five tyres to potholes. (ABC News: Erin Somerville)

The busy real estate agent has spent more than $7,000 and weeks without her car in the past year alone after five tyres were damaged by potholes in separate incidents on Victorian roads.

"VicRoads, when I contacted them, simply said, 'Well, you have got your insurance; it's not our problem,'" she said.

"There's no compensation whatsoever, which I think is pretty bad when we all have to have our cars roadworthy and we all pay registrations … but then the roads aren't worthy for us."

Andrea Lever ripped her tyre on a pothole in July. (Supplied: Andrea Lever)

The latest pothole she hit in July was marked by Mr Panozzo, whose work she appreciates, but she was unable to avoid it due to oncoming traffic.

She said she worried about her younger staff on the roads.

"It was big, and it made such a loud bang," she said.

"I kept reflecting on that moment, thinking, is it going to be a fatality next?"

title: Five decades in the making, a Garma announcement has an eye to the future
text:
On the escarpment at Gulkula, in north-east Arnhem Land, a historic announcement was made that could transform the economic future of a people and their place in Australia.

At the Garma Festival, the annual event held on Yolŋu land in the remote Northern Territory, dignitaries gathered last weekend to hear Gumatj elder Djawa Yunupiŋu's keynote speech.

In a bombshell moment, Mr Yunupiŋu announced plans to create a new Yolŋu land council, the Dilak Land Council, which would be the first of its kind to be created in the NT in 35 years.

So, what could a new land council mean for Arnhem Land, and why is its announcement so significant?

Turning point for land rights

The significance of the announcement was made even greater by the fact it was presented on the 50th anniversary of the Commonwealth's Aboriginal Land Rights Act (NT), which passed in 1976.

The act was foundation legislation aimed at enabling Aboriginal people to start properly receiving benefits from their own land, after decades of disempowerment.

Charles Darwin University historian Robyn Smith said the act's passage followed "successive decades of protest and advocacy by Aboriginal groups for recognition".

Robyn Smith says NT land rights legislation followed decades of protest and advocacy. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The 1960s and 1970s had seen the Aboriginal rights protest movement come to the fore, with landmark moments including the Wave Hill Walk-Off for Aboriginal workers' rights in 1966.

Another catalyst that led to the act's creation was the high-profile Milirrpum v Nabalco Pty Ltd NT Supreme Court battle over the encroachment of mining on the Gove Peninsula in 1971.

It was a moment seen as pivotal for raising national awareness of the land rights fight, and one which left the elders — including Djawa Yunupiŋu's father — heartbroken when they lost.

From 1972, Australia was being overseen by Labor prime minister Gough Whitlam, who Dr Smith said "was very conscious about social justice".

"His view was that Australia wasn't complete or whole unless or until Aboriginal people were recognised and became a central part of the Australian nation," she said.

Gough Whitlam pours soil into the hands of Vincent Lingiari, symbolically handing the Wave Hill station back to the Gurindji people in 1975. (AGNSW: Mervyn Bishop)

Whitlam triggered a royal commission into Aboriginal land rights in the NT, headed by Justice Edward Woodward — who'd been a senior lawyer for the Yolŋu elders in the Milirrpum v Nabalco case — who in turn recommended that legislation be drafted.

Before the Aboriginal Land Rights Act (NT) could be finalised, Whitlam was spectacularly rolled from government — but his Liberal successor, Malcolm Fraser, saw it passed into law.

Land councils created in the NT

From out of the newly formed act, land councils were created in the NT, to help drive economic empowerment and distribute royalties from major projects on Aboriginal land, like the now-defunct Ranger uranium mine on the edge of Kakadu National Park.

In 1976, the Northern and Central land councils were set up, and they were followed by the formation of the Tiwi Islands land council in 1978.

The fourth and most recent land council to be created in the Territory was the Anindilyakwa Land Council (ALC) on Groote Eylandt in the Gulf of Carpentaria in 1991.

The Anindilyakwa Land Council was established in 1991, becoming the NT's fourth Aboriginal land council. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Former ALC deputy chief executive Matt Houston said he believed "the establishment of the ALC has been one of the most significant milestones in the modern history of Aboriginal land rights and the Anindilyakwa people".

"At its heart, it has been about self-determination," he said.

"The ability for traditional owners to govern their own affairs, make decisions about their own country and represent themselves through their own locally-governed land council."

The ALC's establishment came as Groote Eylandt opened its doors to mining, with the island home to, in Mr Houston's words, "one of the world's largest and highest-grade manganese deposits".

A portrait in Katherine of Vincent Lingiari, who led the Gurindji strike at Wave Hill in 1966. (ABC Rural: Max Rowley)

"[It] reinforced the importance of ensuring the Anindilyakwa people had a strong, locally-based land council to represent their interests in negotiations over land access, mining and the management of royalty income," he said.

The ALC has not been without its challenges in recent years, amid ongoing anti-corruption investigations into issues centred on its now-sacked chief executive, Mark Hewitt.

Yolŋu looking to the future

Similar to Groote Eylandt, Mr Yunupiŋu's Gumatj people and the 13 clans of the Gove Peninsula have the possibility of future major mining projects happening on their land.

It's also a crossroads-era for the peninsula, which is facing the impending exit of the region's biggest employer, a Rio Tinto bauxite mine where operations are scheduled to conclude in 2029.

Yolŋu clans on the Gove Peninsula are also waiting in the wings for a major Commonwealth payout, after the High Court last year ruled in favour of the clan groups in a major native title case.

Djawa Yunupiŋu, centre, says the proposed new land council would work with government and industry to advance the status of Yolŋu people. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

In Mr Yunupiŋu's words, a future land council run by the Yolŋu people would be able to "give new life to the land and the people".

"It will work with government, and with mining companies and any company who wants to do business with us," he said in his Garma speech.

A standalone land council would bypass the need to go through the Northern Land Council, giving the Yolŋu landowners the ability to directly make decisions for their own people.

Malarndirri McCarthy will have to sign off on any new land council if a formal application is made. (ABC News: Billy Cooper )

But there is still a long way to go, and significant hurdles to overcome first.

Another of the Gove Peninsula's key clan groups, the Rirratjiŋu, has initially rejected the idea of joining the Dilak Land Council, but has left the door ajar for future consultations.

New land council plan surprises elder A key clan elder on the Gove Peninsula has voiced his frustration, confusion and concern over a bold plan to create a new Aboriginal land council in his region.

Any future land council would also need to get the tick of approval from the Commonwealth's Indigenous Australians Minister, Malarndirri McCarthy.

"If a formal application is received, the minister will need to consider the detail of the application, stakeholder views and relevant matters," a government spokesperson said.

"The federal government is committed to engaging with traditional owners, communities, land councils and governments to support self-determination and empowerment."

With an eye to the future, Mr Yunupiŋu acknowledged there was still much to be done to bring the land council to life, and said he would "continue to engage" to try and see it through.

title: Retro game pinging, popping and buzzing as new generation has a ball
text:
The highs and lows of pinball have Tash Anderson hooked.

She tried the niche sport more than three years ago after she moved from Albury-Wodonga to Townsville and quickly rose through the ranks.

"I participated in the Women's Masters, which is the biggest women's pinball competition in Australia and ended up coming first, which was super surreal," Ms Anderson said.

Netherworld in Brisbane has pinball machines ranging from retro 1970s models to newer machines. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Social events and competitions in Townsville, such as pizza and pinball nights, have created a vibrant pinball scene enjoyed by an eclectic mix of attendees.

"I've had opportunities to move back to my hometown, and I would do that except for the fact there's no pinball down there," she said.

"If you don't like it, you're not going to come back to it but once you like it, you're in, you're set.

" You're probably not going to be able to live without it. "

Training at home is not an option for Ms Anderson as pinball machines cost thousands of dollars, so social events are her only chance to refine her skills.

"Once you get into a flow state, is what we call it, once you start doing really well and you're reading the machines and the ball correctly, it's a feeling unlike any other," Ms Anderson said.

Pinball enthusiasts attend events and play games at Netherworld, an arcade and diner in Brisbane. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

" A lot of these machines are like a book that you have to read front to back. "

Popularity growing across Australia

Alexander Henrickson is the Queensland representative for the International Flipper Pinball Association, which runs state and national championships.

He said the number of new participants was booming, especially in areas including Townsville and Brisbane.

Alexander Henrickson assists with organising and running Queensland and Australian championships. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"It's become a really nice social event for people to come into and see each other, people make an event of it," he said.

While welcoming the fresh increase in popularity, Mr Henrickson hoped for more women to take part in the competitive sport.

Ms Anderson agreed.

She estimated women accounted for 25 per cent of the current competitors and hoped that would increase to 50 per cent.

One of those is Natalie Dahl, who was introduced to pinball more than three years ago after a friend brought her along to a social pinball event.

Natalie Dahl plays pinball during a social competition at Rising Sun FPV in Townsville. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"It fast became an addiction and a really nice group of friends to play games with," she said.

" We're very lucky in Townsville, we've got a variety of machines in the community. "

Ms Dahl enjoys the challenge, regularly attending local women's competitions.

"It's really good for the brain and the fine motor skills and quite often you just want to beat yourself and do better," she said.

'Labour of love'

For some Townsville residents, the passion for the game is all-consuming.

Chris Sommerville spent the past five years building his own pinball machine.

"I probably could've bought three or four machines with the money that I've put into here — and that's just money, not time," he said.

Chris Sommerville already has three commercial pinball machines at home. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

He said the machine was fully playable, with its own rule set, and he had started installing ramps and plastics as part of what he calls the "beautification stage".

Once completed, he said he would add it to his home collection of three commercial machines.

Sheridan Griffin has a two-and-a-half-month-old baby, but that has not stopped the new mum from competing.

Sheridan Griffin says the pinball scene was male-dominated when she started playing. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Secured in a baby harness, the mother and daughter duo competed as one, with Ms Griffin looking over her daughter's head to play.

"She's been enjoying all the pinball lights, and she's not been too grumpy," Ms Griffin said.

She takes her baby to social pinball events for women, and says the others are very understanding.

Since returning after a four-year break, Mc Griffin has seen more women participating in the thriving pinball scene.

"It's [gone] from really hardly anything, no tournaments or no one talking about it to all of a sudden we've got like three or four different locations in Townsville now."

Mr Henrickson attributed some of that growth to Ms Anderson.

"I love what Tash has done for the scene up in Townsville. I think she's an amazing spokesperson for the sport," he said.

He said he hoped it would make Ms Anderson eligible to participate in the Women's World Pinball Championship next year.

title: Strikes at the country's largest port this weekend could cost millions
text:
Strikes at Australia's largest bulk export port this weekend could cost mining giant BHP $100 million in revenue and the West Australian government upwards of $7 million in royalties, industry bodies say.

Those high numbers reflect the stakes in the ongoing dispute between the miner and unionised members of its workforce in WA's Pilbara.

The industrial action could potentially do what union's have threatened since June: grind a significant portion of shipping from Port Hedland to a halt.

A 24-hour ship loading ban starts today, followed by an additional 24-hour general stoppage tomorrow as part of the months-long dispute with the mining giant over workers' pay and conditions at the port.

How important is Port Hedland?

BHP ships all the iron ore it produces in Australia through Port Hedland — the world's largest bulk export port, nestled alongside a town of about 17,000.

"There are essentially two classes of maritime ports: there are bulk and there are container ports," Curtin University associate professor Elizabeth Jackson said.

She says bulk export ports ship commodities, like iron ore, mineral sands and grains.

The scale of the port's throughput is difficult to understate.

According to Pilbara Ports data, of the more than 800 million tonnes of commodities that left the ports in the last financial year, Port Hedland accounted for 580 million, almost three quarters.

Commodities exported via the Pilbara were valued at $150 billion, with many billions of dollars of that flowing directly through Port Hedland each month.

Port Hedland is the Pilbara's second-largest town. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

Who controls the port?

The latest available data shows the port is home to 19 operational berths. Eight belong to BHP, five to Fortescue, four to Pilbara Ports, and two to Roy Hill.

It takes about 1,200 workers to keep the port running, with about 450 of those employed by BHP and covered by ongoing bargaining negotiations.

Of those 450 workers, 236 were eligible to vote in their unions' respective ballots — that is, unionised workers.

Operations at BHP's Iron ore port in Port Hedland. (ABC News: Charlie Mills)

Dr Jackson said Port Hedland shipped more than the next three biggest ports combined.

"It is by far and away the largest [bulk export port] on earth," Dr Jackson said.

"Industries, construction, all sorts of manufacturing, automotive vehicles … if it contains iron ore, it's probably come from either Port Hedland or Dampier."

Where does the ore go?

That iron is transported in bulk carriers — vessels some 300 meters long that hold hundreds of thousands of tonnes of ore — to steel hungry customers overseas.

"The biggest customers from Port Hedland in terms of iron ore? Number one, China, by far and away China," Dr Jackson said.

A bulk carrier is loaded with iron ore at Port Hedland. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

"Number two, the Republic of Korea, number three is Japan, and then under that is Indonesia, Taiwan and Vietnam."

BHP's five iron ore operations across the Pilbara are responsible for the mining giant's entire Australian output of the commodity.

The miner produced 290 million tonnes of iron ore on a 100 per cent basis, according to the 2025-26 financial year operational review.

BHP iron ore operations at Port Hedland Port in WA's Pilbara. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

What's happening this weekend?

This weekend's industrial action is a marked escalation, with the 48 hours of various stoppages up from just 8 in July.

Unions and BHP have been negotiating since October last year.

Eleven bargaining meetings later — three under the oversight of the Fair Work Commission — no agreement has been struck.

Electrical Trades Union represents electricians at the port. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

The negotiations span three unions: the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), the Australian Manufacturing Worker's Union (AMWU), and the Western Mine Worker's Alliance — a partnership between the Australian Worker's Union (AWU) and the Mining and Energy Union (MEU).

Today, the AWU will participate in a ban on ship loading over 24 hours, and tomorrow join their ETU and AMWU counterparts in a work stoppage.

Tomorrow's action won't have the militant picket lines reminiscent of 2000, but it won't be the family friendly fun day the unions spruiked for the rally in July, either.

An eight-hour strike was staged by unionised BHP staff in Port Hedland in July. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

It's understood the message to workers participating in the renewed stoppage was, "don't come to work."

In separate action, electrical workers at the miner's operations near Newman, about 450 kilometres inland, will also down tools on Sunday, an escalation from months of overtime bans.

BHP has consistently maintained it has contingency plans to limit disruption caused by industrial action, but has not clarified what those plans entail.

Is there a way forward?

A bargaining meeting last week again failed to avoid the industrial action, but responses from both parties alluded to positive progress.

BHP said the movement meant the strike was unnecessary.

"With another meeting scheduled and an updated proposal to come, we have made significant progress with the [Fair Works] Commission's assistance," a BHP spokesperson said.

"There is no need for the unions to continue with their planned industrial action.

“The only thing union-led industrial action will achieve is to further delay a fair and reasonable deal."

BHP's Port Hedland operations. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

And while unwilling to call off the strike, the union message also pointed to a potential resolution.

"The meeting was productive," a Combined Ports Unions spokesperson said.

"And while substantive issues are yet to be resolved, the parties have identified a path forward which we will pursue over coming weeks."

The next meeting before the FWC is scheduled for August 18, with BHP committing to tabling an updated proposal.

title: AFL issues Cats a 'please explain' over defender's concussion contract
text:
Geelong has been handed a belated 'please explain' notice from the AFL after initially avoiding sanction over its controversial secret deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, a player with a history of concussions.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who on Friday evening identified himself as the player in question, whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

The bombshell concussion case emerged on Thursday and pressure mounted on the league and Geelong after the AFL didn't hand down any punishment that night.

On Friday afternoon, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had signed off on the deal and confirmed the 'please explain' notice.

Geelong's Steve Hocking said the club would provide information to the AFL about Kolodjashnij's contract. (AAP Image: Erik Anderson)

"I take responsibility for the fact that we didn't lodge it with the AFL and the (AFL)PA," Hocking told reporters in Geelong.

"… I have received a letter of 'please explain' from the AFL in relation to this matter, so we'll deal with that over the coming days."

Hocking said not registering the deal was a "misstep" and was uncertain what consequences Geelong would face.

"We've got a 'please explain' letter, and at the appropriate time we'll work through that with the AFL," he said.

"We'll have to respond to that, and then it'll be up to the AFL, and whatever that is, we'll accept."

Later on Friday, Kolodjashnij issued a statement through Geelong, confirming he was the previously unnamed player.

"While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally," Kolodjashnij said.

"I participated fully in the AFL's independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since.

"What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private.

"… I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season."

The 2022 premiership defender, 30, has played 209 games.

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, retired prematurely in 2020 due to concussion.

On Thursday night, calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL had insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

Geelong also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

Grief-stricken mother of star footballer reveals AFL executive phone call West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown says AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother says the phone call was "too little, too late".

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board when the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the AFL statement.

Drummond did not front the media and issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Many AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and former number one draft pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham 'Polly' Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multimillion-dollar concussion class action against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

title: In a town families are moving to, an important health service has departed
text:
Leanna Testa was at a mother's group in the outback town of Longreach, in Western Queensland, when she heard about the help other women were receiving for post-birthing issues.

"I was talking to a few mums at the Feral Mums Club about it, just wanting to know with ab[dominal] separation, what I'm dealing with, if it's severe or if it's minor," Ms Testa said.

"One of the mums told me that there was a lady [pelvic floor physiotherapist] out here and that she is amazing."

Leanna Testa was referred to see the pelvic health physiotherapist in Longreach in May, but never heard back. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstrens)

The mother of two children obtained a referral to see the specialist.

"That was back in May, and to this day I've never received a phone call," Ms Testa said.

The Central West's only trained public pelvic floor physiotherapist left the region in July after spending a couple of years based at Longreach Hospital.

One of her previous patients said access to the treatment locally was life-changing.

"She gave me the ability just to function without pain, like just everyday, day-to-day, walking up the stairs, getting in and out of the car," mother of two Antje Dekruyf said.

Jade Miller says she faces an eight-hour drive to see a pelvic health physiotherapist in Rockhampton. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

New resident Jade Miller said she was facing an eight-hour drive to get help with her abdominal separation.

"I did my initial appointment in Rockhampton [before I moved], but because there is no other specialist out here, I can't have any follow-up appointments," Ms Miller said.

"If I do [need an appointment], I have to go back to Rockhampton, which is not really doable with two young children."

Now, women across the Central West face uncertainty about access to specialised care for conditions including birth injury, endometriosis and menopause.

Recruitment underway, specialty skill not guaranteed

Hospital data reveals a growth in the number of births in Longreach, rising by 60 per cent between 2020 and 2025, from 54 to 86 per year, reflecting a community view that the number of families in the region had increased.

Amid the outback baby boom, the Central West Hospital and Health Service (CWHHS) said in a statement it rejected any suggestion it was downgrading pelvic health services.

The Central West Hospital and Health Service says specialist allied health professionals are in short supply. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

"Across Queensland and indeed Australia, allied health clinicians with specialist skills are in short supply and extremely difficult to attract and retain in remote areas, including the Central West," executive director of regional health Craig Carey said.

The CWHHS director said recruitment for a generalist physiotherapist was underway, but he could not guarantee they would have the same level of pelvic health experience as their predecessor.

Longreach has a population of about 3,000 people. (ABC Western Qld: Jay Carstens)

Pelvic Pain Australia's vice chair Alexandra Diggles, who is also a physiotherapist pelvic floor specialist, said that was concerning.

"A generalist physio in a hospital may never have covered or understood any pelvic health concerns," Ms Diggles said.

"Not even attempting to replace that position with a needed service may be a bit of a shortfall of innovation or insight for that health service as well."

Several mothers at local playgroups say they have needed help from a pelvic health physiotherapist. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

It is that potential gap in future services that has local mothers worried.

"When you're dealing with pelvic floor and having to do internal exams, I think it's really important for someone to be very knowledgeable in that area," Ms Dekruyf.

"I wouldn't personally feel comfortable with a generalist [without training] doing that sort of stuff."

Growing industry interest

Pelvic Pain Australia said the role of physiotherapy in managing pelvic pain symptoms was a growing specialty.

"Physios are known for improving muscle function … [especially during] the transition times in life like pregnancy or menopause or after prostate surgery, when there's been a challenge to that system," Ms Diggles said.

The Australian Physiotherapy Association said more physiotherapists were choosing to upskill in women's health, which could ease rural shortages.

The organisation said since launching pelvic health training courses in 2020, 669 physiotherapists had gained the knowledge required for after-birth treatment.

"Women in rural areas shouldn't have to choose between living in the community that they love and having access to the physiotherapy services that they deserve," the organisation's member director Catherine Willis said.

Antje Dekruyf says Longreach is a growing town and deserves to have better specialist services. (ABC Western Queensland: Jay Carstens)

That is something Ms Dekruyf agrees with.

"I think with the growing number of families, it's a necessity, especially because Longreach is the hub [of the West]," she said.

title: After 67 years, Brisbane's Centenary Pool to close for major Olympic upgrade
text:
Brisbane's historic Centenary Pool will close at the end of August to undergo major redevelopment for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2032.

The now heritage-listed pool was first opened to the public in 1959 and became Brisbane's first Olympic standard pool.

The centre reflected a national mania for swimming in the wake of Australia's success in the pool at the 1956 Melbourne Olympic Games, where the host country walked away with eight gold medals in swimming events.

A busy day at the Centenary Pool seen from above. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

The pool was designed by Brisbane City's architect James Birrel.

Mr Birrel passed away in 2019, but his son Jack Birrell, now a Tasmanian-based architect himself, has fond memories of the pool.

"I can actually remember as a child, Dad holding my hand and walking me through the project," Mr Birrell said.

Loading...

"He talked a lot about how his role as a city architect, how he had a sort of ethical and moral obligation to make public buildings not just financially stack up but to be the most they can possibly be for all people."

With its distinctive restaurant "floating" above the water, Mr Birrel said Centenary Pool was a "cultural mecca" in its heyday.

The restaurant above the pool was a popular spot for wedding receptions. (Supplied: Brisbane City Archives)

"All the dignitaries of the day would be seen there, it was a real place to promenade and look out over the world."

Childhood memories

Donna Hansen, 67, grew up in Brisbane's northern suburbs and said she would visit the pool "two or three times a week" in summer as a child.

"We would go from when it opened to when it closed, the whole day," she said.

Swimmers enjoying the Centenary Pool (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

"It was amazing. It was the walk back to the bus stop we all hated, but it was a really good part of my childhood."

Allana French has been coming to the pool for about 40 years.

Ms French said she could recall a distinctive smell from when an Indian restaurant operated at the pool during the 70s and 80s.

"I can remember when you would take a breath and you could smell curries coming from the restaurant."

Fresh from the water, Allana French said she has been visiting Centenary Pool for about 40 years. (ABC News: Stephen Clarke)

Greg Mahony, 79, used to visit as a schoolboy on Saturdays.

"It was all good fun, jumping off the high tower. I tried to teach myself a bit so I wouldn't be embarrassed at the annual swimming carnival," he said.

" All the young ones would be there and get out of the pool and sunbake on the concrete. "

On September 1 the centre will be handed over to the Games Independent Infrastructure and Coordination Authority (GIICA), the body responsible for delivering the venue infrastructure for the 2032 Games.

Centenary Pool will form part of the new National Aquatic Centre, which will include three new pools and permanent seating for 8,800 attendees.

Centenary Pool's diving tower inspires memories of terror and excitement in equal measures. (Supplied: Brisbane City Archives)

Mr Mahony said he hopes the site remains a community swimming pool while also helping to "continue Australia's swimming domination".

Olympian Mark Stockwell won three medals for Australia in swimming at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympic Games.

He was instrumental in pushing for a redevelopment of the pool in the 1990s and just a few years later the centre was listed on Queensland's Heritage Register.

Olympic swimmer Mark Stockwell. (ABC News: Cameron Lang)

He hopes the pool will continue to be looked after and preserved for the community as it enters the "third stage of its life".

"It was a gift from the Queensland government to the Brisbane City Council and to the people of Brisbane for its centenary back in 1959," he said.

"I think that's an important history, and it's an important thing to preserve."

title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
text:
Grammy Award-winning British musician and producer William Orbit, who worked with artists including Madonna, Britney Spears and U2, has died aged 69, his family and friends said on Friday.

The London-born musician, who won two of his three Grammys for production work on Madonna's 1998 album Ray Of Light, died at home on July 23, according to their statement posted on his Instagram page.

"We are deeply saddened by his passing. He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," it stated.

As well as helping Madonna move into electronica and trip-hop with the 1998 hit album, Orbit also worked with the US star on 2000's Music as well as co-writing and performing on her 1999 single Beautiful Stranger.

The track, which appeared in the second Austin Powers film, earned him another Grammy for best song written for visual media.

Orbit was also nominated for Grammys for his work on Pink's song Feel Good Time, his own 2000 album Pieces In A Modern Style and for record of the year for Ray Of Light.

He also produced for Britpop band Blur, girl group All Saints and Spice Girl Mel C.

She paid tribute to Orbit on Instagram, posting that it was "such an honour to have worked with this great man".

Meanwhile Nicole Appleton of All Saints posted: "He was a treasure in the music industry and we had the most amazing times in the studio and socially. We will forever celebrate him as a music icon."

Orbit also worked with Britney Spears and will.i.am on the 2013 album Britney Jean and produced two songs that featured on U2's compilation The Best Of 1990–2000.

He had a solo career which produced 12 studio albums, largely electronic music, and was also a member of the groups Bassomatic and Torch Song.

AFP

title: ‘A torpedo’: Italy-Spain border blow-up now a major headache for Europe – and Australian travellers
text:

Analysis WorldEuropeRefugees ‘A torpedo’: Italy-Spain border blow-up now a major headache for Europe – and Australian travellers David Crowe August 8, 2026 — 11:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A sudden move has deepened a border dispute between Spain and Italy that could delay thousands of travellers moving between the countries – and erode a pivotal agreement on passport checks across Europe. Spain has called on Italy to lift border controls that it imposed last week following a rush of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Migrants returning to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July. AP Italy has refused to relent after being given a Sunday deadline to drop its additional controls, and Spain has retaliated with measures of its own. The result is the rapid imposition of passport checks on many travellers moving directly between the two countries – something not seen in decades.

Advertisement

Tempers are running hot. Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares described the Italian border policy as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”. Speaking on Friday in Europe (Friday night, AEST), he said that Madrid was prepared to respond with a tough approach of its own. Hours later, it did just that. This is now a major headache for the European Union. And travellers from Australia. Italy has suspended the usual rules for travellers from outside the European Union who arrive from Spain, declaring that it needs the stronger safeguards until at least August 15. Spain has decided to do the same for those who arrive from Italy. This applies from midnight on Saturday – 8am on Sunday, AEST – at Spanish borders. So, officials will conduct passport, nationality and visa checks for Italian passengers and visitors from other countries arriving from Italy.

Advertisement

Australians travelling between the two countries will need to be on guard for additional controls. What began as a diplomatic dispute about Ceuta is turning into a test of the Schengen Agreement that was signed in 1985 to waive passport checks on travellers moving across the internal borders of most EU member states. Loading At its best, the Schengen Agreement allows the citizens of 29 member countries to move easily across their borders without a passport check, visa or electronic travel authority. For visitors from Australia and other countries, it also ensures relatively seamless travel across those internal EU borders. Once the traveller arrives at the first Schengen member state and clears passport control, there is usually no need for any other passport check when moving to other member states inside the Schengen zone.

Advertisement

This has been so successful that the initial agreement of 1985 was codified in a convention in 1990 and extended many times to the point where the Schengen zone now has a population of 450 million people. The latest expansion came last year when Romania and Bulgaria joined in full. Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right For Australians on longer journeys, the only challenge with the Schengen zone is making sure they don’t visit for more than 90 days in any 180-day period – the basic rule that often leads to side-trips to non-Schengen states such as Britain or Ireland. (While Ireland is in the EU, it never joined Schengen.) But now, Schengen is under some strain. The argument between Italy and Spain comes amid other tensions at European borders. The new digital Entry/Exit System, or EES, has led to long queues at passport control for non-EU nationals, who must be registered with the new system.

Advertisement

Travellers have missed flights because of sluggish checks at border control kiosks, where officials gather fingerprints and photographs to enter each person into the vast new database. It is an operational failure. The workaround at some airports is to halt the EES for a period and return to old ways of clearing queues. A 12-year-old who crossed into Spain is escorted by a Spanish soldier to the Spain-Morocco border this week, as the child begs not to be sent back to Morocco. AP The new argument about Schengen, however, is foundational. It is about whether Schengen has become a point of weakness for Europe when so many are concerned about illegal arrivals and asylum seekers. Political leaders are responding to clear signals that voters want lower migration. Spain insists that the concern is overblown. Its latest estimate is that 72,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco in the final days of July. It says almost all of them returned to Morocco. Crucially, Ceuta is not in the Schengen zone. Adult migrants who get to Ceuta have to clear other checks before they can reach the European mainland.

Advertisement

Thousands of the migrants are still in Ceuta, though. Spanish authorities have confirmed about 1100 unaccompanied minors are still in the enclave and have a legal right to remain. They are likely to be transferred to Spain. Related Article Aviation ‘Bring food and water’: Australians face six-hour lines for Euro summer Even so, Italy will not drop its concern about illegal migrants getting to Spain and taking advantage of easy travel across borders into Italy. So Spain has chosen to retaliate. In practical terms, this means Italian officials check passports for non-EU citizens arriving from Spain. Since there is no land border between the two, it entails checks on flights from Madrid, Barcelona, ​​Ibiza, Valencia and other Spanish locations, as well as some ferries. Italy appears to have an agreement with France to have stronger checks on land border crossings, but it is not clear what difference this makes.

Advertisement

The Spanish response appears likely to mean additional checks on all travellers arriving directly from Italian airports. Related Article Immigration ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave Travellers moving through other Schengen states should not see any change – not for now, at least. But everything depends on whether the argument between Italy and Spain spreads to their neighbours. What if other countries decide they too want to erect barriers against arrivals from Spain because of the anxiety about migrants in Ceuta? As right-wing leaders in Europe demand bigger and stronger borders, it will be tempting for governments to toughen their policies, even if Spain insists that it has the problem under control.

Advertisement

For the moment, Italy and Spain are set to intensify their fight over national pride and border policy by making queues longer at their airports. And by punishing travellers. title: ‘The club went too far’: AFL chairman apologises over concussion contract saga
text:
AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond has apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation” amid the fallout from the league’s concussion contract saga.

On Friday, Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of a secret concussion deal with the club, which was scrapped this week after the AFL said it did not approve it.

AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui

Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and is insisted he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level.

On Saturday, Drummond, who was the Cats’ president when the deal was signed, said in a statement that despite getting agreement from Kolodjashnij for the secret deal, “the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed”.

Penrith coach Ivan Cleary confirmed after the game: “It doesn’t look great.” The 31-year-old is expected to undergo scans on Sunday, with the worst-case scenario to end Yeo’s season – and more than likely his dreams of captaining Australia to a World Cup win on home soil. Loading Leniu was saddened to hear the Yeo news when informed in the sheds after the Roosters’ gritty 20-18 win over Canterbury on Friday night. “No way. That’s a massive loss – he’s the heartbeat of their team,” Leniu said.

“Knowing Penrith, they’re a world-class team, and they’ll have that next-man-up mentality. “They’ve done it the last couple of years, they fill those voids when it comes around, and it will be no different next week if he’s out. Loading “He’s the captain, and when a lot of experience like that goes off the field, you definitely notice it. “But Penrith are a well-oiled machine. With that next-man-up mentality, if you get the tap on the shoulder, you’ve got a duty to perform and wear the jersey with pride.

“That’s been the Penrith Panthers the last few years. That’s why they’ve been such a great team. Another perspective Opinion

Next week will be another day in the office.” The Panthers won 40-4 against the Roosters in round three when Tom Jenkins raced in four tries. But the Roosters have won their past seven games, and are building momentum at the right time. They are also set to welcome back skipper James Tedesco from an ankle injury. “I’ve got a lot of confidence in this team, the boys inside the four walls have confidence in each other, it was a scrappy win [against the Dogs], but we got the win,” Leniu said.

Naufahu Whyte has been a standout for the Roosters, and in Leniu’s opinion is on track to be crowned one of the Dally M props of the year. “He’s a no-nonsense player, he comes into training, if you ask him how he’s going, he’ll tell you, ‘same old, same old’,” Leniu said. “That’s who he is. He goes about his business, he doesn’t try to be anyone else but himself, and flourishes when he goes out there.”

title: The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass Paul Cully August 8, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’ first Test as Wallabies coach could easily turn into the shocker in Osaka. The heat and humidity they are likely to encounter is one factor, but aside from that, Japan are a competitive Test side underpinned by an improving domestic competition filled with high-quality coaches from around the world. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Les Kiss chat at training ahead of Saturday’s match against Japan. Getty Images The Brave Blossoms were messed around by Ireland’s recent refusal to travel to Japan in the Nations Championship, but they have won the scheduling battle for this two-Test series against the Wallabies. Kiss would have copped the odd hospital pass as a player. Now, as a coach, he’s got a high ball well above his shoulders with Eddie Jones steaming in from 20 metres away.

Advertisement

The Wallabies could lose this Test. The bar for success in Kiss’ debut as coach is a win of any nature: get the job done and get out of there. It is a Test with a high-risk profile, and Kiss was never going to be able to fully mitigate that risk, no matter how he selected his team. Loading However, his 23-man squad and the make-up of the bench have increased the likelihood of Japan getting away to the fast start they desperately want. Josh Canham and Miles Amatosero are a young pairing, and they will face Warner Dearns, the best second-rower in Super Rugby Pacific this season, while prop Aidan Ross is more solid than spectacular and certainly won’t offer the same mobility around the field as Angus Bell.

Advertisement

Jones has prioritised speed from the outset, preferring Jack Cornelsen in the second row ahead of Harry Hockings, and Amatosero is going to be tested by the speed of the game if Japan get the quick ball they want. Clearly, the Wallabies’ strategy is to finish the Test strongly with their stacked bench, but they won’t want to be chasing the game with the combative Hockings and that old warrior Michael Leitch providing serious nuisance value off the bench for Jones. Eddie Jones and Japan will be ready for the challenge posed by the Wallabies. Getty Images The Wallabies must have considered the opposite approach – trying to overwhelm the Japanese early. That is something the French did well in June. Japan probably don’t even know themselves what a good side they are, but their self-belief will soar if they start well and exert scoreboard pressure on the Wallabies.

Advertisement

A Japan XV side put themselves in a great position against the Maori All Blacks in late June, racing into a 24-7 lead at halftime during their game in Nagoya, before that lack of self-belief kicked in. They were chased down and lost 38-31. But they will have learnt something from that defeat and young No.10 Ryunosuke Ito probably banked some valuable lessons as he continues his crash-course introduction to Test rugby. Loading The other player to look for is Japan No.6 Ben Gunter, who is on a big collision course with Wallaby Rob Valetini. Gunter, who grew up in Australia, has arguably the biggest shoulders in Test rugby and is not afraid to use them. He has snuck under the radar this week with all the focus on Hockings, but Gunter is the better player. He is an old-fashioned hitman who will also be lining up Harry Wilson if the Wallabies captain comes off the back fence.

Advertisement

The Jones factor is also inescapable, and the former Wallabies coach will have some clear views on how and where Kiss’s side can be vulnerable. Related Article Australian rugby Hoop dreams: How growing up on a court turned Josh into a Wallabies ‘baller’ But it’s a factor that is easy to overplay in a rugby world in which the degrees of separation between Australian rugby and Japan are decreasing anyway. For example, new Wallabies defence coach Scott McLeod almost won the Japan Rugby League One title in June (against Dave Rennie’s Kobe) as an assistant at Kubota Spears. In a classic clash of styles, Kubota employed a kicking and defence-based game plan, using the tactical nous of new/old Waratahs No.10 Bernard Foley.

Advertisement

Against Rennie’s ball-in-hand style – and Kobe superstar Ardie Savea – it almost worked too: Kubota might have won the game but for a knock-on by former Crusaders halfback Bryn Hall with the tryline in sight. That decider was a good showcase for the tactical variety and physicality of the Japanese game, and their players are increasingly well-prepared for the demands of Test rugby. Kiss, therefore, has been handed a tricky first assignment – and if he marks it with a victory, it is a bigger positive than he will get credit for.
