title: My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss
text:
Advertisement

NationalGen Z Opinion My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author August 8, 2026 — 9:30am

August 8, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I can’t believe,” says my daughter as I navigate our rented manual car around the narrow, cobbled streets of Nazaré, Portugal, “that you used to have to read maps to travel.” As the gears grind yet again under my rusty touch, I glance at her and laugh: “But we were using a whole part of our brain that you guys don’t touch now.” She shrugs, tapping on her phone. Illustration by Dionne Gain Remember maps? Calling from a phone box? Aerogram letters? Post-school travel for those born in the ’70s meant disappearing into Europe like a gumboot into quicksand, swallowed whole by different cultures. We were not being monitored, surveilled, tracked: we were finding our own paths, new ones. We didn’t have mobile phones with location data, downloadable maps, apps to make bookings. This, too, confounds my daughter: “But your parents wouldn’t know if you were dead.” I guess they just waved us off and hoped for the best. There was something delightful about the invisibility, being out of range and absolved of all responsibility. We were just gone, and we’d be back in a few months. Sure, I’d call home every week or two – collect, to the eye-rolls of my parents – and send the odd postcard, but that was it. We took photos on little cameras and mailed the film back home to be developed: they were unfailingly blurry, unflattering, often tilted or poorly framed. But it wasn’t about how we looked, it was about what we were looking at. There are few things as genuinely thrilling about entering and inhaling a new country for the first time. We took terrible risks, sleeping on beaches, train stations, boat shacks, all to save money, and relied on overnight train trips to get some rest, zigzagging around the continent with a heavily stamped Eurail Pass.

Advertisement

My daughter and her friends are too smart to do stupid things like sleep in public places. But I watch the reels and feeds of this Euro-generation, who save up and go year after year to the prettiest places in Europe, navigating swelling crowds, and I am gobsmacked. Julia Baird in Venice during her own backpacker adventure. First, they look so good. Polished and picture-perfect. I think I packed a hairbrush, but I can’t be sure. Maybe an eyeliner? Nothing more. I was gripped by an Oscar Wilde biography (the superb work by Richard Ellmann) and was somehow inspired by that to invest in several vintage Spanish brocade jackets which were hopeless in the cold and probably looked half mad, paired with scuffed Doc Martens and cut-off jeans. Today I scroll through Instagram and see a string of girls in bikinis and impeccable, tasteful clothes. Carousels of cute poses. Second, there is an ease to travel we did not know, facilitated by the phone and by the now-widespread fluency in English across Europe. If we didn’t make an effort to learn the local language, we were cooked: Google Translate didn’t exist. According to travel research group MMGY’s 2025 Portrait of European Travellers (surveying France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK), Gen Z (aged 14-29) is responsible for the travel boom in Europe, and is planning to spend more on global travel and take more vacations than any other age bracket. Unsurprisingly, Italy, Spain and Greece are considered the most desirable, while the US flags in popularity. They are using planning tools and AI to map out itineraries.

Advertisement

But tech isn’t just aiding travel, it’s shaping and changing it. The most picturesque, Insta-worthy places are swamped by young people looking for the perfect shot to post, much to the annoyance of locals. Sweating crowds in sweltering Europe jostle around landmarks and crowd the most photogenic vistas. Today in the centre of Lisbon, where I have come to research a book, on the way to the train station I wove past dozens of people in Instagram poses, hands on hips, laughing, tilting heads, pouting, flexing. What they are missing is the joy of not being seen. Of waking up on beaches with panda eyes, not worrying someone will take a shot and post it. I remember speaking a year ago to one teen who was preparing for a Mediterranean trip by having her eyelashes, nails and brows done: “No way am I going to be chopped [look unattractive] in Greece,” she said. The prevalence of social media has also led to milder behaviour, according to a 2024 survey by youth travel agency StudentUniverse. It found only one in five young Australians planned to party when travelling overseas: 84 per cent of Gen Z full-time students scheduled trips where there would be no drinking. Many parents would cheer, given the genuine concerns about drink-spiking and safety, but 27 per cent of Gen Z also said they just didn’t want to be snapped doing something embarrassing.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Tourism Idiots are ruining travel for the rest of us Ben Groundwater Travel writer StudentUniverse’s Will Jones told Student Traveller this trend – of “dry-trippers” – had been rapid and widespread: “This is the first generation to be setting this trend. I’m a Millennial and I remember when I was their age having holidays focused on drinking and partying. So it is amazing how much, and how quickly, this has changed. “Australians used to be seen as big party people, but this Gen Z is the first global generation. Because of social media, they all seem to be following the same trends and doing the same things.” This is a generation that is having less sex, drinking less and reading fewer books (although they are reading in digital formats). But they are travelling more often. War or global instability haven’t deterred them, with only 1.5 per cent of Australians under 30 cancelling trips to Europe in 2026. Home ownership is hard, almost impossible; holidays are within reach.

Advertisement

In 2023, The Guardian declared “gritty gap years” were out and “grand tours of Europe’s charisma” were in. Is it weird to be nostalgic about the grit? A time when we could run wild, unobserved, learning how to fend for ourselves? When we could just have fun – or not – instead of feeling like we also had to look like we were having fun? I realise this makes me seem ancient. I also feel like I’m describing the daily life of ancient explorers. But in trading concealment for convenience, evaporation for ease, surely we are in danger of losing the pleasure of forgetting ourselves and truly paying attention, marvelling. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: How grace changes everything. title: Fifty years of friendship: How I saw the world beside a poetry great
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Driving along the expressway up to the Blue Mountains under heavy grey clouds, the end of one of Robert’s poems came to me: “This blustery wind/brings rain – just/short hairs/ on a barber’s sheet,/marking the windscreen”. I thought too that barber’s sheets in the 1970s, when I first met Robert, were usually white, but now it’s reversed, the sheets are black and my hairs are all white. Artist Tom Carment’s 2009 portrait of poet Robert Gray. Palings Record Store 1975. Robert and I were flicking through album covers, rows of them arranged in boxes alphabetically. I looked right towards D and noticed a young woman pull out Bob Dylan’s Blonde on Blonde and frown in concentration at the album notes. “She looks like a nice girl,” I said to Robert. “Wait a sec,” he replied. I looked across and soon he was standing next to her with one hand in the pocket of his tapered John and Merivale jacket, the other elegantly gesticulating. He was smiling, relaxed, and a couple of times she looked shyly in my direction. Robert walked with her back to where I’d been standing. “Marguerite would be happy to go on a date with you.” I shook her hand, blushing. The next weekend I drove 20 kilometres to her family home in Elanora Heights, where she introduced me to her father, the minister at a local church. We had an early dinner in Chinatown, and I drove her home by the 10pm curfew. A few days later I received a neatly written two-page letter saying how much she’d enjoyed our date. It was signed, “Yours in Dylan, Marguerite”. From time to time I remember that letter, and it pains me to recall that I never wrote back. In the mid-1970s Robert met his life partner Dee, who had a daughter, Harriet, two years old. Dee was working as a hairdresser then and saved up her money to buy Robert a teal grey Olivetti Lettera portable typewriter, the epitome of elegant Italian design. He loved this small machine and sometimes took it out with him on the ferry to Manly to work on his poems. He sat there for hours, he told me, traversing the harbour back and forth, on a single fare. Forty years later Robert finally started writing on a computer, but soon the tremor from his Parkinson’s disease made it too hard to manage the sensitive keyboard. His old Olivetti had been given away by then, so I lent him my Hermes Portable typewriter. He was confident it would provide a solution – he could pound its keyboard with his shaking hands. Last week I took it back home again. I don’t think he ever used it. Harriet, Robert Gray and Tom Carment at Urunga Baths in 1984. Dee Jones Robert never drove and he loved to be a passenger on a car journey or on a train heading north, watching the landscape pass by out the window. He had a white scar on his nose which he sometimes hid with one hand, the result of a bad car accident he told me, from when he travelled up to Queensland in the 1960s with landscape painter Lance Solomon. Another time he said the accident was in Sydney and that he’d woken up in hospital and refused a blood transfusion, in unconscious deference to his Jehovah’s Witness family. A few times in the 1970s I drove Robert up along the Pacific Highway to Coffs Harbour, where he’d grown up, and where I’d first met him, in my cousin Diana Wood Conroy’s house on a bush block north of Bellingen.

Advertisement

One summer afternoon, as we looped through the tall eucalypts outside Bulahdelah, the windows of my EJ Holden down (no air-conditioning), Robert pulled out a notebook, screwed up his face and started writing. The cicadas outside were extremely loud – it was one of those bumper years. He shouted across to me, above the din, “The cicadas sound like someone pouring shells onto a huge pile of shells.” He was always jotting down similes and thoughts in that book, and I’d read some of them, printed, later, worked into a poem. His first few books had many poems about journeys, homecomings, almost baroque in their excess of descriptive detail. I loved them. Robert Gray in Pyrmont in 1974. Tom Carment As a child Robert had heart disease and wasn’t expected to live into his 20s but, against his doctors’ predictions, he survived, the hole in his heart grew over. I feel that the outpouring of poems written following this recovery represented his joy at being alive. Sometimes he was criticised for just being a descriptive writer but in my view, his level of observation and looking was, in itself, an unwritten philosophy. In later years Robert grew to dislike the use of similes in these early works and changed most of them into metaphors. He reworked other things too, made numerous refinements, he thought. Robert’s old friend, the poet Jamie Grant, and I doubted this was an improvement. “You’re a different man now,” I told him, “with a different voice. I don’t go around repainting all my pictures from the 1970s and 80s.” He disagreed and defended his editing eloquently, citing Walt Whitman’s constant revision of his opus Leaves of Grass. Once, as I sat next to Robert at a friend’s funeral, he whispered to me that he was itching to edit the words of Abide with Me. We were both autodidacts, browsers, with no tertiary education. When I first met Robert he’d already had a book of poems published, Introspect, Retrospect (Lyre-Bird Writers 1970), which he told me he no longer liked and would steal from libraries, to destroy. After he died Dee and I found a copy of this slim, blue, saddle-stitched paperback in his desk drawer, every page of type covered in a spiderweb of pencilled corrections. On weekends we often went walking and drawing together, carrying our A3 cartridge paper pads into the bush. Dee and Harriet would usually come too and we’d catch the train or cram across the bench seat of my Holden ute and head up to the Blue Mountains, Cowan or along West Head Road for a bushwalk. Afterwards we’d stop at a milk bar and drink cool vanilla malted milkshakes out of battered aluminium containers. At Bundanoon we rented old back-pedal brake bikes near the station and hid them in the bush before walking down to the edge of the cliff face. One day we made a pilgrimage to D. H. Lawrence’s house in Thirroul, Wyewurk, where he lived in 1922 and wrote the novel Kangaroo. We went down steps to the rocks below the house, where Lawrence and his wife Frieda would have gone swimming, and started drawing, looking south. An elderly man came up behind us to watch and after a while said: “Drawing are you? It’s a great sport!” Robert Gray on NSW’s North Coast rail line in 1970.

Advertisement

Fisher Library 1979: A book entitled Gout and Goutiness in the medical section, marked the place to turn left, down the corridor to the Fine Arts section towards the books you’d never see in a bookshop, in German, French and Italian about Caspar David Friedrich, Corot, Gericault, Paula Modersohn-Becker and many more. Robert had recently worked there and had a borrowing card which he rarely used, preferring usually to reshelve these wonderful books after we’d looked at them. Sydney University’s Fisher Library Stack, the section where books were kept for post-graduate use, was our Nirvana. We were both autodidacts, browsers, with no tertiary education. Robert was nine years ahead of me in his reading and life experience and I was trying to catch up. He often lent me poetry books from his own shelves: Elizabeth Bishop, William Carlos Williams, Thomas Hardy, Edward Thomas, D. H. Lawrence, Philip Larkin, with a pencil tick on the contents page to mark the ones he liked best. I once said to him (perhaps ungratefully) that I’d rather not see these ticks, I wanted to discover what I liked by myself. He was offended. I guess in some ways I was his protégé in those days, a role from which I slowly withdrew. In the 1970s he liked coming over to view my latest paintings and drawings and was always confident in his opinions, telling me what he thought was an advance and what was a backward step. “This one’s a real breakthrough!” he’d say with excitement. I recently re-read some letters he wrote to me then, in which he expounded his theories: “To be an expressionist is essentially a linear talent. To try and be an expressionist with colour leads to terrible excesses…” I didn’t always agree, but he had a very good eye. Sorting the good from the bad, in writing, art or film was not a trivial matter for Robert – it was life or death, with no middle ground. He was always making lists of best artists, best films, and the reverse. After he died Dee and I found, written in one of his notebooks from the 1980s, a list: “Worst painters consistently given a lot of wall space: Renoir, Chagall, Georgia O’Keeffe.” Tom Carment sawing wood at Bellingen in 1974. Diana Wood Conroy Royal National Park 1982. We stopped for a break at Wattamolla and sat on some rocks near the sea, pulling out our wrapped lunches, a Granny Smith apple in each one. We’d started our journey before dawn at Central Station – our goal was to walk from Bundeena to Otford in one day, 28 kilometres. Robert took a bite from his green apple and dipped it in the sea and then another, and dipped it again. On that hot day the salty tang was great. “My father used to do this,” he said. We walked on, refreshed, looping over headlands where the path was cut deep into the headland like a WWI trench and through the palm forest above Burning Palms. The sun was getting low and Robert checked his watch and saw that we’d have to speed up to get the next train from Otford, to avoid an hour of waiting in the dark on the platform for the next one. So we started jogging along the narrow track. “Keep your eyes about you,” he shouted back to me, and I knew his meaning was not to watch out for trip hazards but to keep observing things as much as we had when walking slowly – the shape of the angophoras, the lichened rocks and the arching eucalypts, all rushing past us. After 50 years of shared experiences, there was no need for him to put on a good show, or impress me. Robert rang up and asked if he could help our oldest son Felix with his HSC English. He’d just finished editing (with Geoff Lehmann) a big anthology of Australian poetry and now had some free time. The allotted poet that year was Gwen Harwood. Felix and I cycled over to the Rose Bay flat and laid out seven poems by Harwood on the pine dining table, worn pale on one side by Robert’s writing arm. For nearly two hours he patiently analysed them with Felix, line by line, succinctly and in plain language. As we were leaving he confessed to me that he wasn’t previously much of a Gwen Harwood fan, but “now I like her a lot better.” A few years later Robert himself was selected as poet for the HSC English students and a slim paperback of his selected poems, entitled Coast Road, was printed in a large edition. Robert chose my painting Morning, Scotts Head for the cover – houses by the sunlit sea.

Advertisement

Tom Carment’s 2018 painting Rose’s Olivetti in Don’s Shed. Robert was diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 20 years ago and the illness increasingly clamped down on his body and his mind. He never complained about having got it but railed against its restrictions. I visited more regularly. I think he felt comfortable with me there. Old arguments were put aside and our friendship entered a new phase of honesty. After 50 years of shared experiences, there was no need for him to put on a good show, or impress me. By 2024 he often left a sentence hanging in the air, unfinished. I could sometimes guess where it was going, and, if not, I valued the fragment. Some days I slowly translated the text from his French art books. If you live long enough it isn’t death you fear

but what life can still do.

(from Robert’s poem about his mother, In Dying Light) A few weeks before his death, Dee had caught the flu and so I went in to the Waverley nursing home, Illowra, to feed Robert his lunch, small spoonfuls of the soft, aged care food. He ate more dessert than mains. It was hard for him to move or speak by then, so I tried to amuse him with anecdotes from our mutual past: the greasy breakfasts we’d been served in 1974 at the People’s Palace in Brisbane (I ate both), the afternoon we’d been dive-bombed by swallows above the water reservoir near the Thames, the boat trip to Den Haag to see Vermeer’s View of Delft. Robert Gray, in his Rose Bay home in 2008. Quentin Jones. After a while Robert shook his head, said, “No more, thank you,” and pushed my hand away; “Tom… I’d like to ask you a favour”. I leaned in to listen as he gathered energy for the next sentence. “Could you hail me a taxi to Central Station? I need to take the train to Bellingen.” “The train doesn’t go through Bellingen,” I replied, “We’d have to get someone to pick us up from Coffs Harbour, or Urunga… and today’s North Coast train has already left the station.” I rolled the food tray away towards the window and, while my back was turned, he swung his thin legs away from the bed. Before I could catch him, he’d launched himself forward and crashed to the floor. As a teenager Robert’s favourite piece of descriptive writing, he told me, came from Robert Louis Stevenson’s Treasure Island – the scene where Jim Hawkins shoots the murderous Israel Hand. The sailor falls dead into the shallow sea and sinks slowly until his body lies huddled on the bright sand. “Sometimes, by the quivering of the water, he appeared to move a little, as if he were trying to rise.”

title: The simple $174,000 question many retirees still get wrong
text:
Advertisement

August 8, 2026 — 5:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I was asked a simple question on social media this week, one that most people in the retirement and superannuation industry think people already know the answer to. But to my surprise, it sparked an enormous conversation. The question was “If I’m retired why wouldn’t I just take all my money out of super and put it in the bank?” Apparently, many people are unaware of the benefits of keeping their money in super, and don’t know about the really juicy upside of moving your superannuation into a retirement phase account so you can enjoy tax-free income when you’re retired. So today we’re going back to basics – to what actually happens to your money the day you retire and why that decision, more than almost any other that you’ll make determines how far your retirement savings might stretch. A question of super. Simon Letch While you’re working, your super sits in what’s called the accumulation phase. Most people reach retirement today with a reasonable or even large balance in their accumulation phase account, unable to access it until they meet two key conditions: reaching the official superannuation access age of 60, and ceasing just one job/employment relationship (even if they go back to work elsewhere afterwards) or, or simply turning 65 at which point you can access your super unconditionally, whether you’re working or not.

Advertisement

During your working phase of your life, you contribute to your superannuation account chiefly from your employer contributions, which are taxed at up to 15 per cent on the way in up to the concessional contribution cap of $32,500. And once the money is inside super investment earnings are taxed at 15 per cent and capital gains at up to 10 per cent because superannuation still gets a one-third discount on assets held longer than 12 months. Why on earth does the bank feel more compelling? I think it comes down to familiarity. But from the day you retire you’re allowed to move some or all of that money, up to $2.1 million, into a retirement phase account, sometimes labelled a retirement pension, account-based pension or income stream, depending on your fund. And the minute your money lands in this account, you benefit because the earnings on that money becomes completely tax-free. There’s no income tax payable and no tax on the capital gains. And moreover, you can draw money out at any time either as a lump sum or as a regular income stream that can feel much like a pay cheque, though funds do require you to draw down a minimum amount each year, once you’re in the retirement phase, starting at 4 per cent of your balance if you’re under 65, and rising as you get older.

Advertisement

That means every single dollar your investments earn inside your retirement account is yours to keep, and if your investments are growing, you can let them compound even more strongly than they might have in an accumulation account where the taxman would take 15 per cent out in tax on earnings each year. Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Why your bank might be overcharging you interest – and how to check Bec Wilson Money contributor When you move your money from an accumulation account into a retirement account, it stays invested – and you still have choices around how it’s invested and how much risk you want exposure to. But if you stayed invested in the same things, and just switched accounts, the returns for the retirement phase would be higher, simply because of the tax. Now compare that to the bank account that my community member was tempted by. Every dollar of interest you earn from a bank account gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your full marginal rate. If you’ve still got a part-time wage coming in or any other income sources kicking along outside super that could mean handing 30, 37 or even 45¢ in every dollar to the tax office. Inside a retirement account, that growth will cost you nothing.

Advertisement

Let’s compare the latest returns on superannuation funds in both the accumulation and retirement phase, which Chant West released just over a week ago, with how someone who’d put all their retirement savings into a bank account. Chant West’s own data shows exactly what that tax difference is worth to someone’s hip pocket. Take the Hostplus Balanced fund. Held in an ordinary accumulation phase account it returned 8.9 per cent a year over the 10 years to June 2026. Held in the retirement phase, the same investment strategy, same fund, same underlying assets returned 10.1 per cent a year. That’s a gap of more than a full percentage point every single year purely because of tax. Compound that over a 25 or 30 year retirement, and it’s the difference between having enough or rationing your money carefully to make it through the last decade. To bring this picture to life, I asked Chant West’s Ian Fryer to run the numbers for someone retiring at 65 with $500,000 in their super, drawing the minimum required 5 per cent a year for the next 10 years, using the returns from mid-2016 to mid-2026.

Advertisement

If that $500,000 had gone into term deposits instead, drawing the same 5 per cent out every single year, the retiree would have ended their decade with about $404,000. On the surface that looks OK, but once you strip out the inflation rate, that $404,000 is really only worth about $299,000. In real terms their savings had gone backwards by more than a third. Now, let’s compare that with the same $500,000 left in a typical balanced retirement account inside super, invested with around half in growth assets and drawing the same 5 per cent a year. Based purely on that those funds were targeted to earn, which is usually CPI + 2.75 per cent, they’d already have finished the decade ahead, at around $521,000. And because balanced super funds have actually beaten their own targets over the last 10 years, the real-world median returns leaves that retiree, 10 years later, with $579,000, which is worth about $427,000 once you adjust for inflation. Stop and think about it. That’s the same starting balance, and the same amount drawn from super every year for 10 years. The only thing that changed was where the money sat – either in a term deposit at the bank or inside a retirement phase superannuation account. The gap between the two is $174,000 in nominal terms, or roughly $129,000 once you account for inflation. That’s tax-free compounding in action.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Opinion

Home loans Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor So why on earth does the bank feel more compelling? I think it comes down to familiarity. People understand bank accounts and term deposits - they’ve had them their whole life. They can log in, see their money sitting there and sleep at night without the markets moving around while they sleep. Super, by comparison can feel like a bit of a black box, run by someone you don’t know as well, invested in things you’ve never really understood. And the balance can move around in ways that make you uncomfortable. And then there’s the fear of the government tinkering with it, something that is increasingly coming to the fore in every education session I run. If you feel that way, you’re clearly not alone – thousands of people on Facebook felt the same this week. But there’s more to learn about super as you approach retirement because in the retirement phase it does something exceptional – it grows, completely tax-free. And that might be more valuable than you’d ever contemplated.

title: Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market
text:

MoneyPlanning & budgetingHome loans Opinion Three steps to protect your home loan from a falling market Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor August 8, 2026 — 5:01am

August 8, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Directly after the federal budget on May 12, I began my column with the words: “Didn’t anybody drafting last week’s budget think of the 95 per cent first home buyers?” The budget – and its controversial tax changes – was ostensibly about helping younger Aussies onto the housing ladder by removing the artificial property inflators of negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount. It was meant to suppress the property market. Escalating interest rates have meant many are struggling to keep up with their mortgage repayments. Gabriele Charlotte The problem was that this was just after the government enticed a whole heap of first home buyers into the market… with just 5 per cent deposits. In my post-budget piece, I wrote: “In October last year, the government pulled the trigger – three months early – on a hugely expanded Home Guarantee Scheme, which allows first home buyers to purchase with a 5 per cent deposit and avoid expensive lenders’ mortgage insurance.”

Advertisement

This is usually payable below a 20 per cent deposit but, under the scheme, the government goes guarantor for 15 per cent of your property so you can avoid that insurance, which is often tens of thousands of dollars. But, as I wrote: “After paying your 5 per cent, leg-up-onto-the-ladder deposit, you take on a debt that is rungs and rungs higher than you otherwise might: 95 per cent.” Prices will, ultimately, start rising again. It’s just a matter of riding it out. And on October 1 last year, the allowable purchase price of the Home Guarantee Scheme was significantly lifted to include a bunch more properties and the means test abolished, to allow a bunch more first home buyers. In fact, all of them. Well, guess what? In the past week, debate has flared – in light of a smallish market retraction so far – about just how many newer home owners now owe more money than their property is worth.

Advertisement

The Coalition says tens of thousands of the 60,000-plus first home buyers who entered the market in that first six months (not all of whom used the scheme), are at risk of falling into negative equity, though the total number across all home owners remains under 1 per cent. Editor's pick Home loans This is how many home owners are actually in negative equity now So if you think you might be at risk, let’s get to the vital steps to avoiding negative equity stress. Firstly, where property prices will land remains to be seen. But it’s worth remembering that most existing investors will simply hold on – their perks are too good to give up and the blanket nature of the CGT rules (to the government’s credit) makes no competing investment more attractive (although super remains attractive). Underpinning property is that investors are far from panic selling. And that’s similar to what recent buyers need to avoid: being forced into pressure selling.

Advertisement

An asset’s value is only on paper; that value is only realised if you need to swap the asset for cold, hard cash. And the single key to avoiding that is being able to – ongoing – afford your repayments. That’s, of course, in the context of three rate rises so far this year. Pure and simple, it’s about your outgoings and your income. In the cost-of-living squeeze, recent home buyers in particular will have squeezed outgoings to the extreme – that’s part of what you have to do to qualify for a mortgage (especially a 95 per cent one!). But don’t miss either that to get a loan over the line, you must also pass a 300 basis-point interest-rate stress test. That means the lender has assessed that you can cope with 12 rate rises, where there have only been three. So, with the outgoings side of your life-ledger possibly sound, how secure is your income? Because losing this is the big risk you want to mitigate. Can you take steps to shore up your job? Do they recognise the contribution you are making? Perhaps you could even upskill to become more valuable to the business. The other employment unknown is illness or injury and there is insurance available for this: income protection.

Advertisement

Income protection is expensive but it is tax-deductible. You can also reduce its cost significantly by opting for a long wait period before it would begin to (75 per cent) replace your pay. And that’s where an emergency fund comes in. This can also subsidise you for the time until income protection insurance kicks in. Editor's pick Property prices End of the super-cycle: Big call on the national property market Indeed, the ideal is to have six months’ salary stashed – which may well be a pipe dream. But – for safety – just start squirrelling away what you can (for flexibility and access, the best place is in an offset account beside the mortgage in question). If it’s too late for all that though, know that your lender is required to have a dedicated hardship department that must extend you concessions if you get into financial strife. Instead of missing a repayment, as counterintuitive as it sounds, tell your lender you will struggle to make it beforehand. They’ll help – at least for a time.

Advertisement

Besides, missing a payment will affect your credit score. Entering a hardship arrangement with a lender will not; that arrangement will only be noted on your credit report, and not flow through to your score, for 12 months. The other thing to appreciate is that, even if you have found or do find yourself in negative equity, it should be brief. Prices will, ultimately, start rising again. It’s just a matter of riding it out. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. title: What happens when crime is no longer paying for our real estate?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesResidential property What happens when crime is no longer paying for our real estate? Colin Kruger August 8, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paying $15 million for a penthouse, even one with views of both the Sydney Harbour Bridge and Opera House from the outdoor hot tub, is feeling very 2025 as the slump in houses became a national phenomenon this week. Sydney and Melbourne are down more than 5 per cent from their peaks, according to property data group Cotality, while the property booms in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth are now deflating as well. The luxury penthouse was seized under proceeds of crime laws and was sold for millions less than its previous purchase price, despite a rising property market. But the buyers of the luxury penthouse in Sydney’s historic The Rocks district must have felt they got a bargain with its purchase last year, given the same property changed hands for $17.5 million in 2018. But the real winner appears to be the buyer of the sub-penthouse who picked it up for $9.4 million a few months later. It had changed hands for $14 million in 2019.

Advertisement

Both properties had been acquired at these questionably high prices by the same party, but the original owners had a lot more to grumble about than the multimillion dollar losses on the two transactions. In 2020, the two properties were put under a restraining order by the AFP-led Criminal Assets Confiscation Taskforce (CACT) - a team set up to confiscate the illegal wealth and assets of organised crime syndicates. Related Article Exclusive

Crime Underworld loses Sydney mansions, jewels, cars worth $1b in AFP raids CACT successfully seized the properties in 2024 as a result of Operation Cabestro, a Melbourne-based investigation into large-scale fraud involving imported alcohol which defrauded federal coffers of hundreds of millions of dollars. The multimillion-dollar losses on the sales appear to confirm that money launderers are not that picky about the price, as long as their ill-gotten gains get converted into respectable wealth - and potentially with a capital gain to boot.

Advertisement

To give an idea of how popular money is with our criminal class, since 2020, police have frozen about $1.2 billion in criminal assets. Two-thirds of that is related to property. Not any more. The criminal world’s free ride from rising property prices has been cruelled - as it has for the rest of us - via higher interest rates and changes to the tax treatment of capital gains. The tantalising question is, what additional downward pressure has there been on housing prices from the changes to anti-money laundering provisions last month which means tens of billions of dollars in criminal proceeds now have to find a new home? On July 1, real estate agents, accountants and lawyers came under Australia’s Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act for the first time. It means these parties will now have to know who their buyers and sellers are in any transaction and report any suspicious activity to police. A buyer can no longer just roll up to the selling agent with a boot load of cash and scant identification, no questions asked.

Advertisement

Australia’s financial crimes watchdog, AUSTRAC is in no doubt what impact this will have on house prices. AUSTRAC boss Brendan Thomas has said previously that it pushes up house prices and takes “property that would otherwise have been purchased by a hard-working Australian”. AUSTRAC CEO Brendan Thomas says criminal gangs are using professional enablers and shell companies to store illicit funds in the Australian real estate market. Max Mason-Hubers The Melbourne proceeds of crime that ended up in a Sydney penthouse will be much harder to carry out in this new environment, Thomas says. “We expect the reforms will bring more cases like this to light and help uncover money laundering in real estate transactions, that we don’t currently see, by bringing suspicious activity to our attention earlier,” he said.

Advertisement

But not everyone thinks it will have an impact on your average home price. “From a price perspective, we don’t expect a major impact - property values are still driven by supply, demand and interest rates,” Dr Nicola Powell, chief economist at real estate portal Domain, says. “What these reforms will do is lift transparency and add more rigour, particularly in higher-value or more complex transactions,” she says. AMP’s chief economist Shane Oliver says there doesn’t appear to be any reliable estimates of the value of money laundered through property, but it looks to be less than one per cent of transactions. He said it’s likely biased towards the upper end of the property market, which appears to be under most pressure at present from rate hikes and the tax hike on investors.

Advertisement

“So I suspect on its own the tougher regulations would only have a very minor impact, but coming at a time when there is already downward pressure on property prices, they may have the impact of magnifying the weakness particularly for upper end property and suburbs,” he said. Nicola Powell, Domain’s chief economist, says new anti-money laundering laws are not having a significant impact on property prices. Renee Nowytarger Reports from Canada, which also had a flood of criminal money funnelled through its Pacific Rim property hot spots like Vancouver, also equivocated on the potential impact. While an earlier study from 2019 found that criminal money may have raised prices in British Columbia by 5 per cent, a 2022 Cullen Commission report found that money laundering is not a significant cause of housing affordability issues or rising real estate prices. “While the impact of money laundering and anti-money laundering measures on real estate prices is something that would benefit from further study, I am unable to conclude that money laundering is a significant cause of housing affordability in the residential real estate market,” Cullen concluded. title: ‘Never seen so many grown men cry’: The everyday Aussies who can’t afford another disaster
text:
Australians are “psychologically unprepared for the world we are moving into”, writes Professor Clive Hamilton in 2024’s Living Hot: Surviving and Thriving on a Heating Planet . “We urgently need a sustained national conversation … about where we live and how we live as the Earth takes us way outside our climatic comfort zones.”

There are thousands of such stories across the country, unique in their details but with a common thread: Australians are confronting the consequences of global warming now, and it will get worse in our lifetimes – or our children’s lifetimes. Whether you talk to climate scientists, insurance companies, and even some politicians, the message is the same: we are doing far too little, far too slowly, to adapt to a climate that has already changed and will be unrecognisable within a generation or two. Governments across the country make commitments and adopt plans, but routinely fail to fund or follow through.

Tweed Shire mayor Chris Cherry says after several big floods “we need to just face up to that and accept that we need to adapt.”

Scene three: The Tweed Shire, in the far north of NSW, is used to floods. Mayor Chris Cherry rattles them off: 2017, 2022, 2024 and then ex-tropical cyclone Alfred last year. The visitor centre in Murwillumbah was destroyed in the floods of 2017 and, despite works to fortify it, was again “completely annihilated” in 2022. It’s been moved to higher ground. People are on the move, too, with 175 government “buybacks” approved so far of Tweed homes deemed impossible to defend. There’s pressure for more housing. Cherry says, “The community is crying out for reducing the standards and building in places that we normally wouldn’t allow, just because it’s easier, and it’s cheaper land … but we just can’t relax those standards because then we’re just making the same mistake all over again.”

Scene two: Just after 9am at a Darwin cafe, 30 degrees already and heading for 33, Phil Blum and fellow members of the Darwin cycling club recover after a two-hour ride. It’s April, the brutal summer months almost behind him, but Blum, a doctor at Royal Darwin Hospital, isn’t sure how much longer he can deal with the heat. “It’s too hot, and it’s getting hotter,” says the 58-year-old of the capital city with the highest temperatures and humidity in the country. “In 50 years, it will be unliveable.” Blum’s family once opened the doors to let in the breeze; now, they close them. “We use air-conditioning six months of the year, all the time, night and day.” He plans to move south in the coming years. “You don’t want to be having to hide in the air-conditioning all day.”

S cene one: Bayden Bedwell feels trapped. In the raging October 2022 flood that swept through Greater Shepparton, the worst in the Victorian regional city in more than a century, water rose 40 centimetres above the floor of his three-bedroom home. Insurance was enough to repair it to the way it was, but the house is as vulnerable as ever in a city named in one study as the most susceptible to flood in the country. Bedwell, 28, says “you can still hear the cracking of everything at night”. He and his wife Chloe would like to move their two young children somewhere safer, but they’re stuck – a house on the same street was for sale for nine months, he says, “then went really, really cheap, about $90,000.”

Climate science is imprecise, but 2 degrees of warming will be far worse than 1.5, and credible estimates indicate the world will sail past that red line around mid-century, less than 25 years away, with close to 3 degrees predicted by the end of the century. Australia’s first climate-change risk assessment report , released late last year, clarified what we face. Australia “experiences compounding and cascading hazards, and this is going to increase”. One example: by mid-century, more than 1.5 million people will be living in areas of high-sea-level rise and coastal flooding.

It’s been a decade since 195 parties, including Australia, signed up to the Paris Agreement to work to keep global warming to “well below 2 degrees” – with the aspiration of holding it to 1.5 degrees – to avoid the worst impacts of global warming. (President Donald Trump has withdrawn the US, the second-highest emitter after China, from the agreement.) Temperatures vary year to year, but climate scientists say that nothing can stop the 1.5 degrees being breached now. Climate change is accelerating. The past three years have been the hottest on record , with 2024 hitting 1.55 degrees of warming. Climate scientists say that the catastrophic heatwave and fires in Europe this year would have been “virtually impossible” without global warming. The “super” El Niño now upon us almost certainly means next year will break another record, bringing devastating heatwaves, storms and bushfires.

Australia has been slow – the government published our first national adaptation plan late last year. It was cautious compared to the UK’s clarion call, containing no strategy or cost estimates, but it did warn that the number of resilience projects across the country is “not high in comparison to the current and projected risks, and the low numbers in high-risk regions, such as in the Northern Territory, suggest significant adaptation shortfall at present”. Dr Russ Wise is a senior principal research scientist at CSIRO and has been prodding governments for 15 years to prepare for a transformed climate. Australia’s adaptation plan was an “incremental first step”, he says. What we need is AUKUS-level focus and funding – up to $15 billion a year, including public and private investment. We need “big strategic thinking and planning in every single region around Australia”.

In climate jargon, preparing to live in a hotter, more extreme world is “adaptation”. It’s different from reducing global-warming emissions through moving away from fossil fuels to renewable energy, for instance – that’s mitigation. The UK’s fourth climate change assessment, released in May – the hottest May on record in the UK – was called A Well-Adapted UK . Greenhouse gas emissions responsible for global warming had dropped in the UK (as they have in Australia) but “there has been little progress on preparing ourselves for the changing climate”, the report said. “Adaptation cannot wait. Keeping people secure is a fundamental duty of the state.” But it would cost – about £11 billion ($21 billion) a year from the public purse and industry.

There’s a hard truth to face, says the CEO of the Insurance Council of Australia, Andrew Hall. “We have spent a lot of money on our own emissions reduction but, in fact, the more urgent challenge we’ve got is resiliency because emissions reduction is not going to make any difference to the climate events we are experiencing … number one is you want people to live in a home that’s not going to get destroyed every five to 10 years.”

The insurance industry’s job is to assess and price risk, and it argues Australia is out of time to start protecting its citizens from the impact of climate change, especially the soaring cost of floods and other natural disasters, which are already eye-watering. Federal spending alone on disaster recovery has more than tripled compared to the early 2000s: in the 2024 federal budget, disaster response projections were $11.4 billion; in the May budget, it was up to $16 billion. States also spend billions each year, heavily skewed towards clean-up and recovery – historically, only about 3 per cent of government spending on disasters goes towards prevention, although that has improved recently.

Scene four: Rania Omar dreads the upcoming summer. The 26-year-old lives in a granny flat in Blacktown in Sydney’s west, a suburb that can be five degrees hotter in summer than Sydney’s CBD, which is blessed by sea breezes. In a heatwave, it can be 8 to 10 degrees hotter. Omar suffers fibromyalgia, a chronic disorder that causes severe pain and fatigue, and heat makes her seriously unwell. “I’m honestly really nervous,” she says. “I have bad days and good days … but I feel like when that heat hits, I will be having no good days at all.” Western Sydney councils participate in Heat Smart and Cool Centres programs, designating local libraries, swimming pools, community hubs and shopping centres as air-conditioned refuges. Over summer, Omar spends most of the time at home, saving expensive air-conditioning for the hottest days, and getting by with a portable fan and a cooling towel. Even taking the bus is hard; most bus shelters around Blacktown and nearby Penrith council areas don’t have shade.

The Paris Agreement aimed to treat adaptation with the same urgency as reducing fossil fuel emissions. But it’s a dull word – adaptation – not sexy enough for a culture war, and until recently the poor relation in climate change. It’s about nuts-and-bolts policy, delivered at scale, to prepare for, rather than react to, the impacts of global warming. It’s about individuals upgrading their homes, community sea walls, banning building on flood plains, government “buybacks” and “managed retreat” from areas impossible to defend, and “greening” cities to cool them down. It’s about where and how we live.

Independent MP Zali Steggall argues adaptation is urgent and requires national leadership through an independent adaptation commission – based on the UK model – to set priorities, oversee funding, manage insurance gaps and report back on how we’re going. (Australia’s first adaptation report was done in-house in the Environment Department and included no funding estimates.) Steggall proposes a quarter of one per cent of GDP be set aside to fund resilience, because research indicates that every dollar spent preparing saves as much as $10 in cleaning up and rebuilding from disasters down the track.

“I agree with this much,” says federal Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen. “Even if the world stopped emitting carbon today, there would still be implications from climate change, and those implications would be very real, and we have to deal with the adaptation to climate change … I would agree that adaptation will be and needs to be an increasing focus of governments around the world.” Where Bowen has a “quibble” is with any suggestion that we should rebalance our priorities towards adaptation over emissions reduction. “Yes, Australia is only 1 per cent of [global] emissions, but most countries are 1 per cent of emissions, and if every country took that approach, then you wouldn’t reduce emissions, and we must reduce emissions.”

Living Hot , the book Clive Hamilton wrote with George Wilkenfeld, was provocative. The authors argue that while emissions reduction matters, we have not confronted the reality that nothing Australia does will stop the worsening impacts of climate change here – to pretend otherwise is “wishful thinking”. They also argue that if governments lead a discussion about what we can realistically save and what we can’t, Australians can flourish – but only to a point. The more temperatures rise, the harder it will be to adapt.

Hall’s view is contentious, but this debate is swirling across the Western world. Support for taking action on climate change remains strong in Europe and in Australia, but there is fatigue, with immediate cost-of-living pain and ebbing political will. Trump called global warming a “con job” at the UN General Assembly last September.

‘Even if the world stopped emitting carbon today, there would still be implications from climate change, and those … would be very real.’

Andrew Hall from the Insurance Council says Brisbane is way ahead, too, in giving residents information. “The council has gotten really good at it; they’ve had to because Brisbane has been, for a very long time, a river with a city problem.” The Brisbane City Council’s Flood Awareness Map provides free details including local history of flooding and aerial maps of your property. NSW’s flood data is available only by region, not by property, although some local councils offer more detail. It’s similar in Victoria, where statewide flood maps are being updated.

Queensland gets credit for initiative. The state’s Reconstruction Authority was established after massive floods in 2011, and is charged with both recovery after disasters and resilience. Its job is to rebuild damaged infrastructure such as roads and bridges to a higher standard than the conventional “like for like” repairs. It’s worth the money. A review of $244 million spent on projects in Queensland between 2013 and 2024 found about $988 million was saved in avoided reconstruction costs – roughly a four-to-one return.

The result is a patchwork, with states doing their own thing – Queensland and NSW have “buyback” programs for homes deemed too unsafe in some areas; Victoria does not, despite pleas from some councils including Shepparton in Victoria, where 80 homes were destroyed in the 2022 floods. The response from the state government was “clearly nothing”, says Greater Shepparton mayor Shane Sali.

The Albanese government is not embracing Steggall’s approach, although after years of Coalition inaction, it gets credit for pushing ahead with a detailed risk report, so at least we know what we face. “We are a federation; that’s not going to change,” says Bowen, whose view is that the federal government can provide a framework for levels of government to work together, but not lead adaptation efforts. That’s up to the states. “The adaptation approach for Cairns does not necessarily need to be decided from Canberra.”

“This is a matter of national safety and security,” Steggall says. “We’re miles behind. If I did a defence analogy, we’ve got the army amassing on our border, and we don’t actually have any capability. We’re hoping for local communities to take up pitchforks to deal with it.”

“There is no central source of truth about the peril data in this country,” says Hall. You should be able to search on the web for a property and “click on a button and say, ‘Overlay the bushfire or the flood risk of this property,’ and you just get it straight away. ‘What’s the heat risk? What’s the high-tide risk?’ There needs to be a way.”

If there is no one-stop-shop for consumer risk, soaring bills tell their own story. A new study prepared for Good Weekend by insurance consultancy Finity found that since 2021, the average home insurance premium has risen 63 per cent to $4680 in NSW, 43 per cent to $4335 in Queensland and 66 per cent to $2646 in Victoria. Not all of it is due to climate change, but Finity principal Stephen Lau says flood risk is the biggest reason for the increases, particularly in northern NSW and in Shepparton in Victoria.

Scene five: Rob Page, 71, the owner of East Bundaberg Engineering in regional Queensland, says flood damage has cost his business close to $1 million. The latest deluge was in March, but the record Burnett River flood of 2013 was “the real killer, my whole complex was underwater up to the roof … I’ve never seen so many grown men cry.” Page says he can no longer get flood insurance for his business, but it wasn’t meant to be this way. In 2023, the federal and Queensland governments approved funding for a 1.7-kilometre concrete levee to protect Bundaberg’s CBD and eastern suburbs. It was ready to go, until Mayor Helen Blackburn withdrew her support, saying it would be too costly for ratepayers to maintain. “It was a no-brainer,” says Page. “If the levee was in place, I wouldn’t have a drop of water.” If it floods again, he’ll walk away. “I’m just getting old and tired of losing money.”

Among the most exposed places in the country is the Northern Territory. In June, the NT government released its first climate change policy, a three-page resilience plan with not a single mention of “heat”. A few weeks before this, residents of Papunya, a small community north-west of Alice Springs, sued the NT government in the Federal Court for failing to protect tenants from extreme heat exacerbated by climate change. Residents were fainting due to dehydration, said their lawyer, while old people struggled to sleep at night. The risk assessment points out that northern Australia is especially vulnerable to climate change.

Heat is relative – 30 degrees in Hobart is a normal day in Darwin. By local standards, Darwin now has between six and eight heatwave days a year, defined as when both daytime and nighttime temperatures are unusually high for at least three days. If we reach 3 degrees of global warming, more than a third of the year – up to 120 days – could be a heatwave. It’s not just heat, either – the NT has just been through five natural disasters in a single wet season.

The outgoing executive director of Environment Centre NT, Dr Kirsty Howey, is unusual in that she argues the environment movement needs to evolve from its single-minded focus on lobbying governments to phase out fossil fuels and increasing renewable energy projects. Those issues are important, but “we are going to be shifting. It’s a dualism with the climate movement, where we’ll say, ‘fossil fuels out, clean energy in and the problem is solved.’ [yet] it’s not solved here because no matter what Australia does with its emissions and its renewable-energy buildout, we’re looking at being unliveable. I don’t even call it ‘adaptation’ any more. It’s just like, how are we going to live here?”

Huge seas in northern NSW caused by ex-tropical cyclone Alfred in March 2025 – the first time in decades that a tropical cyclone threatened to make landfall on that part of the coast. Getty Images

It’s a question those living in flood-prone areas are also asking. The Insurance Council identifies 24 river catchments across the East Coast needing urgent investment. It is lobbying for a flood defence fund of $30 billion over 10 years, to be paid for by the federal government and the states most impacted: Queensland, NSW and Victoria. So far, there is little interest. The insurance industry is preoccupied by floods because that’s where it is most exposed. It estimates that there are 242,000 residential dwellings facing the highest flood risk across Australia, with more than 186,000 – three-quarters of them – uninsured for flood, in some cases due to prohibitive cost.

The industry is reluctant to reveal exactly where those communities are for commercial reasons, but Climate Valuation has taken up that challenge. It’s a company that provides climate risk analysis to property owners and, working with the Climate Council, last year named Australia’s 86 most vulnerable towns and suburbs. It says that these areas are in “critical climate risk zones” and without large investment will become hard to insure, a disaster for those wanting to buy or sell, and economically crippling for these towns and suburbs. The list was topped by Shepparton in Victoria, whose mayor, Shane Sali, says, rightly, that the analysis did not take into account the work his council has done to strengthen resilience – including new infrastructure, flood overlays in the planning scheme and a mapping project that measures the flood risk of every property. The next riskiest towns, according to the modelling, are Ballina and Tweed Heads in NSW, and Belair in South Australia.

‘Making polluters help pay for the damage isn’t a pipe dream but right now, it’s a “buyer beware” market.’ Climate Valuation founder Dr Karl Mallon

Climate Valuation founder and director Dr Karl Mallon concedes the study’s limitations, but says it’s based on the best data available, similar to that held by insurance companies that don’t release it. It’s an early warning sign. “What we said is, ‘Take a very good look at Lismore [a NSW regional city devastated by floods in 2022]. And if you’re in one of these 86 places, you’re just waiting for a flood to hit.’ And that was controversial.” He applauds Shepparton’s efforts and says insurance companies should be required to consider prevention efforts when setting premiums.

Mallon says the insurance crunch has been coming for decades, and it shouldn’t be up to individuals, often on lower incomes, to pay to upgrade their houses; fossil fuel companies should pay their share. “We’ve got a bunch of people in Australia who are suffering, and we’ve got a bunch of fossil fuel producers in Australia and, if you do the numbers, they are responsible … Making polluters help pay for the damage isn’t a pipe dream but right now, it’s a ‘buyer beware’ market.”

In December 2022, the national cabinet agreed that “the days of developing on floodplains needs to end”. That has not quite happened – although more restrictions do apply – in part because the housing crisis means there is intense pressure to build 1.2 million new homes by 2029.

In NSW, the biggest climate risks are floods and coastal hazard – about 85 per cent of the NSW population lives within 50 kilometres of the coastline. NSW Planning Minister Paul Scully says there are “200-odd years of decision-making in NSW, where if we had our time again ... we wouldn’t have let homes be built in particular areas”. The task is huge. Committee for Sydney chief executive Eamon says natural disasters have cost the NSW government an average of $1.6 billion a year since the 2019-2020 bushfires. This is 1000 per cent higher than the $154 million a year in the six years before that. Governments need to “shift their mindsets” to deal with the two great intergenerational challenges – housing and climate change, he says: “We should be treating them with the same level of existentialism.”

The state has made progress. It now embeds climate resilience into the planning laws, funds councils to plant street trees, and this year adopted a Build Back Better policy. The Reconstruction Authority, established by the former government in 2022, has produced a disaster mitigation plan and is working on regional versions for the high-priority flood-prone Hawkesbury-Nepean Basin in western Sydney and the Northern Rivers in the state’s north.

“The government’s taken a very deliberate position after the 2022 independent inquiry into floods that we wouldn’t be building homes on dangerous floodplains any more,” Scully says. But opinions differ about what constitutes a “dangerous” floodplain, and the pressure to release land for development to solve the housing crisis is real. After initially ruling out rezonings planned for thousands of homes in Marsden Park North and West Schofields in western Sydney, the government later decided to allow a reduced number of new homes with “strict conditions”.

A development in Marsden Park with dark roofs and minimal trees and black roads and driveways where temperatures will be high in summer and there will be a reliance on air conditioners in Western Sydney. Janie Barrett

In the Northern Rivers, the NSW government tried a buyback program for homes deemed impossible to defend – by the end of June, 826 buybacks had been completed. A related $100 million Resilient Lands program was meant to fast-track flood-safe land for homes, providing 4382 lots. So far, it is yet to deliver any land for housing. A report by the NSW Auditor-General in May this year was scathing, branding both programs as “not effectively planned before implementation”. Scully concedes the problems, but insists things have improved. NSW is given credit for solid plans, but so far, the funding is not there. “Because of the sheer volume of disasters that have occurred in the last half-decade, there is a growing anxiety among local councils in regional areas that it’s getting out of control,” said Darcy Byrne, president of Local Government NSW and mayor of Inner West Council. “We don’t have enough funding to mitigate risk before disasters occur.”

In Victoria, the government has recently taken over responsibility for flood mapping the whole state and to become the decision-maker when imposing future planning restrictions. Until now, this has been the responsibility of individual councils, one that many were not meeting. Updating flood maps is often controversial among locals who see their home decline in value. In 2022, the shire of Baw Baw completed the mapping but, in the face of a backlash from residents, dropped its planning amendments.

‘We don’t have enough funding to mitigate risk before disasters occur.’ Darcy Byrne of Local Government NSW

Some floodplains are still being developed for housing. In Echuca, one development was approved on a piece of land that was underwater as recently as the 2022 floods. Planner Jane Keddie, the vice-president of the Planning Institute of Australia, said climate adaptation policies in Victoria were taking a back seat to building 800,000 affordable new homes by 2034, “even when an application (to build) will result in more people being exposed to that hazard”.

Victoria’s policies on bushfire resilience in new buildings led Australia, and it allocated $264 million towards adaptation in the 2025-26 budget – though close to one-third of that is going to rebuilding after the summer bushfires in the state’s west. Victoria has eight high-level Adaptation Action Plans, but a recent upper house parliamentary committee report found that “actions identified by the [government’s adaptation] strategy were underfunded and under-resourced”.

The pressure largely falls on local governments – those managing planning schemes and most sensitive to local needs. Melbourne’s Lord Mayor Nick Reece explains the dysfunction: “The federal government has all the money, the state government has all the laws, and the local government has all the problems.” Councils can pass amendments to insist on higher environmental standards than the legislated minimums, but they must be approved by the state government. Six years ago, Reece’s council proposed then-leading environmental rules for new commercial buildings, including mandates for solar energy, and options for cooling, such as green roofs and the retention of mature trees. It had the support of the Property Council, the peak body for the development industry and, says Reece, while upfront costs would be higher, the “payback is extremely quick” because the buildings would be cheaper to run. The amendments went to an independent panel of experts, which approved them in October 2024. Since then – nothing. It sat unapproved on the desk of the state planning minister Sonya Kilkenny. “It’s extremely frustrating,” says Reece. Kilkenny declined an interview.

Firefighters are increasingly faced with “catastrophic” fire conditions - the highest possible level of bushfire danger - such as this 2019 fire in Hillville, New South Wales. Getty Images

The wet season is nearly over and Darwin, Australia’s northern capital, is lush. Large trees emerge from the centres of roundabouts, the sea beyond the northern suburb of Nightcliff sparkles and around the CBD, white high-rise apartments nod to the relaxed air of the tropics.

Look deeper, and Darwin is in trouble. Heat is known as a “silent” killer: major heatwaves have caused more deaths since 1890 than bushfires, cyclones, floods and severe storms combined. It’s not just heat. Northern Australia faces what are called “cascading” risks. In the tired office of Environment Centre NT – the territory government cut its $100,000 funding last year – Kirsty Howey checks her phone. It’s March and she and everyone in greater Darwin has received a “boil water alert” after torrential rain pushed Darwin’s dam to overcapacity and the pump station shut down. Water authorities called it an “unprecedented situation” to avoid contamination. Howey, a lawyer who joined the centre as its head in 2020, ticks off the past few months. First, Cyclone Fina in November, the most intense cyclone system since Cyclone Tracy on Christmas Eve 1974, and “a remarkable early-season tropical cyclone” as reported by the Bureau of Meteorology. Winds were so strong that a section of the Royal Darwin Hospital ceiling collapsed.

Then another “unprecedented” event, according to NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro. On March 7, after what was already weeks of massive rainfall, the Katherine River peaked at 19.2 metres. Residents huddled in schools and patients were evacuated from the local hospital. Hardly a breath was taken before severe Cyclone Narelle made landfall in Queensland, the Northern Territory and Western Australia, an extremely rare event.

“Everything’s falling apart,” says Howey, soon to become the CEO of the Wilderness Society. She knows that sounds hyperbolic but insists, “it really is. I’ve been here [in Darwin] for 21 years. I’ve never seen anything on this scale, and there’s no money.” The NT Environment and Planning Minister, Josh Burgoyne, declined an interview. In a statement, he said that recent floods and cyclones “have demonstrated the importance of ensuring our communities, infrastructure and economy are prepared for extreme weather events”. The government had made announcements including a $100 million Flood Recovery Fund to include early-warning systems, flood mitigation and resilience projects.

James Parry, who was evacuated from Nauiyu, south of Darwin, in March for the second time in the wet season, relives the “rivers roaring” and a crocodile turning up in his backyard before he was evacuated from his home. David Hancock/Skyscans

Scene six: Under a tree at Batchelor, James Parry relives the “rivers roaring” and a crocodile turning up in his backyard before he was evacuated from his home in Daly River, known as Nauiyu, south of Darwin. In March, almost 400 people were evacuated, many by helicopter. They were moved to Darwin before shifting again to temporary accommodation in Batchelor. The damage and mud in Daly River was so severe it would be three months before the last resident went home. That flood was the second in just over a month – Parry, 53, was evacuated twice in a single wet season. It’s time, he says, for the Aboriginal community to move to higher ground, and “get out of the water zone; otherwise we’re going through this every time we get rain, the river comes up.” That idea has been voiced many times, but so far, has not happened. It’s not clear who makes that decision, and who pays for it.

Greater Darwin is home to 159,000 people who love it for its casual lifestyle, the fishing, the spectacular sunsets, the long walks along the beach. It’s hot year-round, but it’s the “build-up” in October and November that is most oppressive, with crippling humidity unrelieved by rain. November is the hottest month, with an average nighttime minimum of 25 degrees and, during the day, an average maximum of 34 degrees which, because of the humidity, feels more like 42 degrees. That is dangerous, and it’s not just about temperature. It was once believed that humans could adapt endlessly to heat – Territorians are proud of their toughness. But a 2010 study co-authored by Professor Steven Sherwood, the deputy director of the Climate Change Research Centre at the University of NSW, put a hard limit on heat stress. A “wet bulb” temperature of 35 degrees – a combination of both temperature and humidity – was the upper limit for human survival because the air becomes so moist, sweat cannot evaporate to cool down the body’s core temperature.

That landmark work has since been refined, especially in real-world “heat chambers” that have found lower limits to heat stress, a 31- or 32-degree wet bulb temperature for even younger people under high humidity, and as low as 23 to 28 degrees for those older than 65. That is deadly, and northern Australia is bumping up against those limits. On oft-quoted study in 2023 found that if global warming reaches 2.7 degrees – highly likely – much of northern Australia faces “near unliveable conditions”.

Sherwood says that at 2.7 degrees of global warming, few people could handle living in Darwin and the health of those who did would suffer. Humans – as well as many native animals and livestock – have not lived under those conditions before. “It tells you that there would start to be heatwaves that people would find very, very difficult to cope with.” Grandiose plans proposed by governments over the years to “populate the north” to 4 or 5 million people make Sherwood “shake my head”. “That might have made sense without global warming, but I think that’s not going to work. I don’t think we move people up there; we’re going to end up moving back.”

If there is a farcical symbol of the Territory’s failure to protect people from heat, it is the 55-metre shade structure over a section of Darwin’s Cavenagh Street, where surface temperatures can reach 70 degrees. In 2017, then chief minister Michael Gunner led a delegation to Singapore, a “green oasis” that could teach Darwin a thing or two about how to flourish in a tropical climate. With him was award-winning NT architect Lawrence Nield, who developed a vision to cool Darwin by 2.7 degrees by mass-planting the right kind of trees, coating black bitumen to cool it down, and creating a Cool Darwin Authority to oversee urban planning. Cavenagh Street was a trial — tropical vines would grow over the structure in about 18 months, a quicker solution than waiting for trees to mature.

What followed was a comedy of errors. The vines chosen weren’t suitable, they were pruned too savagely, and they never grew over the structure. The opposition at the time – now the government – mocked the idea of greening the CBD as a foolish priority compared to crime, health and education. A few months ago, the government announced the vines would be removed.

Sunset in the Northern Territory, which is particularly exposed to global warming and dangerous “wet-bulb” temperatures that are a threat to life. David Hancock/Skyscans

Nield, the architect of Cavenagh Street and now retired to Sydney, looks on in despair. Yes, the vines didn’t work but they should have been replaced by something better, he says – and the need to cool down Darwin remains urgent. “I feel my six years [as NT architect] were wasted,” he says. The local council is doing its best to boost the canopy cover over Darwin, but it only controls 13 per cent of the municipality. It has given away thousands of native trees for residents to plant in their own backyards.

Nield wrote an article back in 2018 headlined “Requiem or Renewal?” about Darwin’s cool-down experiment. He was hopeful then. So, which was it in the end? “I think it’s a requiem,” he says. “There’s very little renewal.”

Clive Hamilton says it doesn’t have to be this way. Preparing for climate change could be a positive story, he says, a national project. We can’t tell China or the US or India what to do on emissions, but we “can make a really big difference to how lives are lived in Australia”. If we get on with it, “it’s a hopeful message.”

title: 'No consultations': Pacific communities shocked by controversial US auction proposal
text:
In brief A US proposal to carve up sections of sea floor close to some Pacific nations has generated controvsery.

Pacific territories controlled by the US have expressed dismay, saying they were not told of the proposal.

A Pacific island leader says there were "no consultations" before the US announced swathes of nearby ocean could be auctioned for deep-sea mining exploration, telling the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency the industry faced strong opposition among his people.

Commonwealth of Northern Mariana Islands Governor David Apatang said the idea had caused great unease across the tropical island chain of some 40,000 people.

The United States alarmed its tropical island territories earlier this year, detailing plans to carve up parts of the Pacific Ocean for mining exploration.

Mining companies see enormous wealth in mineral deposits scattered across the seabed, but the fledgling industry has for years been held back by environmental concerns.

An expanse of US maritime territory near American Samoa in the South Pacific could be auctioned as soon as November, according to official documents.
