Separate tracts of ocean surrounding Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands in the Western Pacific are also under consideration.

"Some concerns include disruption to food security for the people of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, who rely on the ocean resources for their survival," Apatang told AFP.

Washington initially proposed to explore a 140,000 square kilometre block about 200 kilometres east of the territory's capital Saipan.

But Apatang said he was caught by surprise when the US announced in March that a similar-sized block to Saipan's west could be leased as well.

"There have been no consultations with the people of the Northern Mariana Islands," he said.

Deep-sea mining companies want to scour the ocean's abyssal plains for mineral deposits and polymetallic nodules laden with nickel, copper and cobalt.

'Unleashing' resources

US President Donald Trump signed an executive order in 2025 aimed at "unleashing" these seabed resources, stressing the demand in everything from renewable energy to military applications.

Critics fear deep-sea mining will cause irreversible damage, smothering marine life in plumes of waste and disrupting oceanic migrations with the thrum of heavy machinery.

The Mariana Islands, Guam and American Samoa all want at least a temporary ban on deep-sea mining in their territorial waters.

But the US territories — which rely on Washington DC for funding and defence — have little say on what it does outside their 5km maritime boundary.

Guam passed laws this year banning deep-sea mining vessels from calling at its ports, potentially hampering the industry by cutting off a crucial source of fuel and supplies.

Apatang said the Northern Mariana Islands would "consider following suit".

Plans for deep-sea mining exploration are most advanced for a vast sweep of ocean near American Samoa, a US territory nestled between New Zealand and Hawaii in the South Pacific.

The US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management is proposing to hold an auction in November, selling exploration licenses for a 125,000 square kilometre block.

The area borders the vast Rose Atoll marine sanctuary, where endangered species of Hawksbill turtle thrive on vibrant reefs.

Lawmaker Aumua Amata, who represents American Samoa in the US House of Representatives, said she worried deep-sea mining could disrupt fisheries providing the vast bulk of the territory's export earnings.

"I represent our people, and I am confident that a majority of American Samoans are opposed," she told AFP.

The licenses cover preliminary surveys and sampling, with future decisions on commercial exploitation needing further bureau approval.

Money for 'nothing'

American Samoa-based environmental advocate Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka said it was impossible to put a "price tag" on the ocean.

"It's not something you think: 'How much money can you make off it?'."

Former US diplomat Emily Wood has been working with the Guam governor's office to better understand the risks of deep-sea mining.

She said leading mining company Impossible Metals had pledged to share one percent of profits with island communities.

"That's nothing at all, compared to the potential damage they might cause," she told AFP.

Impossible Metals did not reply to a request for comment.

The company has previously stated it will not start mining until it is satisfied it is safe.

Pacific island nations are divided on whether deep-sea mining will deliver economic windfalls, or environmental catastrophe.

Nauru and the Cook Islands are among world leaders in seabed mining exploration, while the likes of Samoa, Fiji and Palau have called for a moratorium on the industry.

The US Bureau of Ocean Energy Management was approached for comment.

title: Infantino wins key backing as pressure over FIFA turmoil refuses to fade
text:
In brief FIFA president Gianni Infantino was supported by African and some American confederations.

By contrast, the Norwegian federation called for Infantino's immediate resignation, signalling his leadership crisis is not yet over.

Beleaguered FIFA president Gianni Infantino has received some much-needed support after over a week of scathing criticism revolving around the now-shelved private investment plan, but there was again a call Saturday for him to resign.

The 56-year-old Italian-Swiss lawyer's position remains far from assured despite support from friends he has made during his 10 years in power, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and leading figures in South American football.

FIFA said it could raise up to US$4.2 billion based on a valuation of US$20 billion for a new commercial subsidiary, called the FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which it proposed would run events such as the World Cup and Club World Cup.

However, old ties have been cut loose.

European football's governing body, UEFA, which he served as secretary-general from 2009-16, is in open conflict with FIFA and on Thursday doubled down on last Saturday's statement, saying it no longer has "confidence" in Infantino.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

UEFA repeated its threat of boycotting the World Cups and one of its member associations, the Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) called for Infantino to go immediately.

"We (NFF) are going to ask the FIFA president to resign now," said its straight-talking president Lise Klaveness on Friday.

Infantino is nigh on certain not to heed such a call and carry on his campaign to be elected for a fourth and final term in Rabat next March.

Infantino, who had spent the past turbulent week amongst friends in Morocco who are co-hosting the 2030 World Cup, is for the moment the only candidate.

The deadline for nominations is 18 November.

There is also a mechanism whereby an extraordinary FIFA congress can be called and a vote of no confidence in Infantino held.

Klaveness, also a lawyer, would be many people's choice as a successor, and also the first woman to be head of world football.

READ MORE FIFA abandons World Cup privatisation plan after fierce backlash

However, Klaveness told AFP her personal ambitions had not played a role in demanding Infantino's resignation.

"We're not there yet," said Klaveness.

"For us, it's now about the issues I just mentioned, and not about particular individuals.

"It would be strange for me to start answering questions about myself, and that goes for everyone," the 45-year-old added.

'Public lynching'

North and Central America's governing body CONCACAF's president Victor Montagliani has been the most oft-cited name in terms of challenging Infantino.

CONCACAF — which includes the three co-hosts of the recent World Cup — had been, along with UEFA, the most brutal in their criticism of Infantino and called for "a comprehensive reckoning with this presidency".

However, there has been radio silence from CONCACAF since the latest FIFA statement backing Infantino was issued on Thursday following an emergency meeting of senior directors in Morocco.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) had also been critical of the manner in which the plan had been handled but, like CONCACAF, kept its own counsel following the FIFA statement.

However, Infantino, who has moved on to Colombia where he attended Friday's inauguration of the country's hard-right president Abelardo de la Espriella in Cali, is not without support.

Photos released by the Colombian Football Federation show a smiling Infantino standing alongside South American Football Confederation (CONMEBOL) president Alejandro Dominguez and the president of the Colombian federation, Ramon Jesurun.

CONMEBOL, which includes iconic federations such as Argentina and Brazil, had on Thursday expressed its "concern regarding the repeated unilateral actions taken" by FIFA.

However, on Friday, the CONMEBOL president told journalists "one cannot ignore the great work" done by Infantino.

"We must continue working for football through dialogue; it is not necessary to always agree," Dominguez added.

Following the powerful Argentine Football Association (AFA) and the Paraguayan federation on Thursday, Infantino also received support Friday from the federations of Venezuela and Ecuador.

Mexico — one of the World Cup co-hosts — also swung behind him.

"The FMF (Mexican Football Federation) supports president Infantino's leadership," it said in a statement.

CAF's executive committee "unanimously reconfirmed its support" for the FIFA president in a statement on Thursday.

The body's decision will have pleased South Africa's sports minister Gayton McKenzie, who had urged African football to resist what he called the "public lynching" of Infantino.

title: AI escaped its testing sandbox and hacked a website. The law is still catching up
text:
In brief A rogue AI model hacked a website. The race to determine who is at fault is underway.

The law is moving to catch up with the rapidly evolving AI space.

Cyberattacks carried out by two OpenAI artificial intelligence models acting autonomously raise a novel legal question: who is responsible when AI goes rogue?

In mid-July, two OpenAI models undergoing testing left their confined environment — a scenario the developers had not anticipated — and ventured out onto the internet, attacking Hugging Face, an AI model-hosting platform.

Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue said Friday his company would not be pursuing legal action at this time.

He added Sunday that the US legal code has to be amended to address such groundbreaking incursions.

"We don't want to end up in a world where everyone is facing cyberattacks all the time because of agents and companies that are creating these agents," Delangue said on CBS News show "Face the Nation."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"So I think it's important for regulators, for policymakers to think about the legal framework of this new kind of technology risk," he added.

In his remarks on Friday, he also mentioned Anthropic, which revealed that three of its models had broken into three different websites, also during testing.

Negligence route

Under US civil and criminal law, unauthorised access to a computer system is an offence.

"If a human OpenAI employee had broken into Hugging Face's systems ... OpenAI would be liable for the employee's wrongful conduct," University of Houston law professor Gabriel Weil wrote in an opinion piece for the Transformer newsletter.

"When an AI agent does it, the law treats it very differently, at least for now," he added.

Matthew Tokson, a University of Utah law professor who focuses on new technologies, had a similar view, saying "we haven't had to grapple with that being formed in anything that's not human, and I don't think courts are likely to be there yet."

The question remains open, however, when it comes to the company that created the model.

"Does 'we didn't tell the AI to do that' end the liability question?" asked Rob T. Lee, head of research at the SANS cybersecurity training institute, in a post on X.

University of Washington law professor Ryan Calo does not believe a criminal case would be likely to succeed.

"The company or individual would have to be at least reckless," he said, explaining they would "be substantially certain the crime would occur and build or prompt the system anyway."

Experts see greater potential for a civil — rather than criminal — case, where the burden of proof is lower.

"Some people think that AI companies should be strictly liable if an AI agent that they deploy totally breaks out, causes damages," Tokson explained.

"Others would prefer to do like a negligence assessment and see if they were actually negligent or if this was just sort of an unavoidable accident or something that couldn't possibly have been foreseen," he added.

In such cases there is a standard of care in product design that judges or juries can use to make a ruling, Tokson continued.

"It's all a bit unwritten because we've never had an AI agent break out of its sandbox and hack other people on the internet before," he said.

OpenAI could rely on the lack of legal precedent if it faced a lawsuit, but those that follow will no longer be able to do so, Calo warned.

Proving that a similar incident could have been anticipated "shouldn't be so hard now that it's begun to happen."

title: For multicultural communities, the Census is about more than population statistics
text:
IN BRIEF Census data informs the funding, access, design and distribution of services for a changing Australia.

When inaccurate or incomplete data is recorded, experts believe there can be serious and sometimes life-threatening consequences.

In 2019, 32-year-old Gia Lam gave birth to a baby boy. Three days later, she was found dead inside her home.

Lam's death was deemed "preventable", according to an inquest released in March by the Coroners Court of NSW. It determined she died from a sepsis infection caused by "multiple failures to diagnose a urinary tract infection".

She was raised in Vietnam and immigrated to Australia around 2010. During her time in hospital, Vietnamese interpreters were not available "during some circumstances", according to the coroner's report.

Priyanka Rai, the executive director of the Australian Multicultural Health Collaborative, said that she has heard of "thousands of stories similar to this".

"In that really, really heartbreaking situation, Gia ... tried to communicate with health services that she was in pain. But there was a gap in that communication, essentially," Rai told SBS News.

"She had a visit by a midwife who did note that she could smell something was off, but she put that down to hygiene, rather than actually trying to look for a clinical cause."

Rai said decisions regarding the funding, availability and allocation of translating and interpreting services — including in healthcare — are informed by the Census of Population and Housing.

The upcoming Census will be held on Tuesday 11 August. The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) will collect data on a person's ancestry, country of birth and whether a language other than English is used at home.

What is the Census?

According to 2021 Census data, an estimated 27.6 per cent of Australians were born overseas, and 48.2 per cent of Australians have a parent born overseas.

Emily Walter is a Census national spokesperson at the ABS and admits that "the Census asks lots of questions" about an individual or household.

But Walter told SBS Hindi that the survey is about "understanding who people are, their cultural background, information about their health and their education and their work status".

"It's all really important information for understanding the community's needs."

Libraries also use information from the Census to build their bilingual book collection and source language support materials. Source: AAP / Sipa USA

Abbas Raza Alvi is the president of the Indian Crescent Society of Australia. He told SBS Hindi that he believes the Census form is "quite complex".

It has up to 66 questions and "sometimes contains words in English that some people find hard to understand", Alvi said.

Online information about the Census is available in 26 languages. People who speak a language other than English can also contact the free Translating and Interpreting Service, which provides access to interpreters who speak more than 150 languages.

How does Census data inform multicultural services?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, school catchment areas, health care, infrastructure, and business. It also maps and tracks the locations of various populations and key demographics.

This year, the Census will include two new optional questions (for respondents aged 16 or older) about a person's gender identity and sexual orientation. That will be used to determine services for LGBTQI+ populations in Australia.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

Researchers rely on Census data too. It's used to study a range of topics including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

Peter Doukas, chair of the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Council of Australia, told SBS News it's important to ensure "that we can collect accurate demographic data about what makes up Australia".

"That will include things like the kind of languages that are spoken at home and the contraction of some of the more legacy communities."

What community leaders want changed

Question 17 of the Census asks where a person was born.

Countries listed on the Census form include Australia, England, India, New Zealand, the Philippines, Vietnam and South Africa. If a person is born in another country, they can specify this in the 'Other' field.

An ABS spokesperson told SBS Chinese that "the countries listed are the most commonly reported countries of birth in the 2021 Census".

According to 2025 ABS data, an estimated 732,000 people in Australia were born in China. That's an increase of 32,000 compared to 2024 statistics.

However, the spokesperson said China will not be listed as a separate response category.

"This is to encourage people to write in China, Hong Kong, Macau or Taiwan in the 'Other (specify)' box."

Census data is used to plan for infrastructure and services such as schools, hospitals, and social support systems. Source: Getty / AsiaPac

Rai said she believes a question about English proficiency should be added to the Census.

"We need more granular data around not just country of birth, but English proficiency ... that's an important metric of defining what multiculturalism means.

"In health systems, we have data, for instance, in Western Sydney, we do have a large population that was born overseas. But we don't know what their level of English proficiency is."

She said that impacts funding for services, including hospital interpreters.

"It's those experiences of feeling like nobody understands what you're saying and your concerns are dismissed, [that] then feed into these ongoing issues where we already know multicultural communities don't engage with preventative health, often have worse outcomes because they appear later.

"We can see why, because accessing care is so difficult."

title: Beyond money and ambition: Meet the young people defining success differently
text:
The future was everywhere at this year's Garma Festival — in the conversations between young leaders, in the children who eagerly reached for the microphone between interviews, and in the questions about what comes next.

Across four days on Gulkula — an ancient ceremonial site on Gumatj Country in north-east Arnhem Land — the sounds of dance, song and conversation moved through the stringybark forests as young Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leaders yarned about university degrees, businesses, diplomacy, culture and community leadership.

They voiced ambition without hesitation. But when asked what success means, their answers went beyond careers and salaries.

Instead, they spoke of family. Of culture. Of language. Of Elders. Of Country.

As children gathered nearby, watching the conversation unfold, Ann-Marie Long, a Badjala, Woppaburra and Torres Strait Islander woman and co-founder of Sandpoppy Weaving at First Nations-led organisation EPIC Pathways, reflected on what the notion means to her.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Success for us is about self-determination, being our authentic selves and in a way that we can celebrate, honour and bring many of our community to the table," she tells SBS News.

When I win, my family wins.

But these personal reflections also raise a broader question: how do we measure progress when success is shaped by more than education, employment, and economic opportunity?

National conversations about improving outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people have often focused on measures such as education, employment and economic participation, with a particular emphasis on youth.

For Ann-Marie Long, success is not something achieved alone. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

Under the National Agreement on Closing the Gap, one target aims to increase the proportion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander young people aged 15 to 24 who are engaged in employment, education or training to 67 per cent by 2031. In 2021, the figure was 58 per cent.

The agreement also recognises the importance of culture, language, connection to Country and social and emotional wellbeing.

For the young people SBS News spoke with at Garma, these are not separate measures of success; they are part of the same story.

Success rooted in Country

Away from the stages and crowds at Garma, young people connect through movement, storytelling and learning — ancient practices that inform identity and culture.

For Joshua Yow Yeh, dance in particular has become a pathway back to his heritage.

The 20-year-old Yugambeh, Bundjalung, Minjungbal, Bayali, Kabi Kabi and Gooreng Gooreng man is a student at the National Aboriginal and Islander Skills Development Association (NAISDA) dance college. He says it's a space where he can develop his craft while reconnecting with culture and learning from Elders, both of which are key to his notion of success.

It's one he's still learning to define for himself.

"I think I'm coming into success. I'm finding success being here at Garma and being at NAISDA. I think that's what I've defined success as, learning culture, getting knowledge from your Elders, and, you know, finding your family and all that kind of stuff," he tells SBS News.

For Joshua Yow Yeh, success has been found through learning culture, building confidence and carrying knowledge forward. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

Nearby dancers sit on the muddy grounds in groups of two or three, adorned in white ochre, some having just performed, while others prepare for what's ahead.

Watching the movement around him, Yow Yeh speaks about the role creativity could play in shaping his future, not only in terms of his career, but as a way to give back to the community.

"I definitely want to be at home back in my Country in Queensland, surrounded by all my community or my mob learning and then also passing on knowledge, passing on culture, tradition, sharing it with everyone," he says.

Pursuing opportunities away from home is part of the journey, but Yow Yeh's connection to Country remains central to his view of success.

It's a perspective that resonates with 24-year-old Meriki Moran, a Biripi, Dunghutti and Gumbaynggirr man and diploma student at NAISDA.

As Garma wound down, people began packing up around him — loading cars and gathering belongings to leave Gulkula.

The movement around the festival grounds reflected a reality familiar to many young First Nations people: pursuing opportunities can mean leaving home, even temporarily, while finding ways to remain connected to where they come from.

Moran describes that transition as difficult.

"Moving away from your family, moving away from the people that you grew up with that you've known most of your life, to a whole new area with a whole new type of people that are around you. You don't know what's going to happen," he tells SBS News.

Meriki Moran hopes to take the knowledge he has gained from Elders and cultural experiences and bring it back to his community. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

But despite the challenges, Moran says he is driven by a deeper calling: to bring the knowledge and wisdom gained through his experiences back to his community

We are strong when we are together. We are strong when we know everything that we need to know about our culture, our language.

"Success to me looks like moving back home, back to Country, taking in whatever I've learnt from Elders from on Country, any knowledge sharing that's being handed down to me and hopefully taking it back home so I can help teach the next generation," Moran says.

For Asha Bhat, CEO of Southern Aboriginal Corporation, that nexus between personal and collective achievement is something she has witnessed through 18 years of working with Aboriginal communities across regional Western Australia.

Asha Bhat, CEO of Southern Aboriginal Corporation, says many young First Nations people she works with do not define success solely by qualifications, employment, or income. Credit: Supplied

She says many young people she works with do not define success only through qualifications, employment or income.

"It is about knowing who they are, staying connected to their culture and Country, supporting their families, and creating a better future for the next generation," Bhat tells SBS News.

Success does not happen in isolation; instead, cultural connection provides a foundation from which young people can pursue education, employment, and leadership opportunities.

Culture is not separate from success. It is often the reason success becomes possible.

Defining 'wealth' beyond norms

For Tianie Scott-Knight, a Yankunytjatjara, Pitjantjatjara, Anmatyerre, Kamilaroi and Wiradjuri woman, success has meant building a career while staying connected to the cultural foundations that shaped her.

She works as the First Nations public diplomacy lead at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and is currently on leave while studying at NAISDA. The 12-month program has given her an opportunity to reconnect with dance while following in the footsteps of her grandmother, Dorethea Randall, who was among NAISDA's first students in 1976.

Tianie Scott-Knight says the understanding of who you are and where you come from is the foundation of success. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

She says success begins with knowing who you are and where you come from.

I think success to me is being connected to your culture, knowing who you are and who your family is and being proud in that, and just owning your truth.

Like Yow Yeh, Scott-Knight has kept her connection to Country and her communities close, while pursuing opportunities away from home. She says her future aspirations include both professional leadership and creating opportunities for younger generations.

"I think I would be, hopefully, one day a First Nations ambassador. [I] have long-term goals to be in that position, but also I would love to see myself in a community role ... uplifting my community and young ones and inspiring them," she tells SBS News.

Her experience reflects the pathways many young First Nations people are navigating — moving through universities, workplaces and institutions while maintaining connections to family, culture and Country.

Professor Chelsea Watego, a Munanjahli and South Sea Islander woman and executive director of Queensland University of Technology's (QUT) Carumba Institute, has spent more than two decades working across Indigenous research and community-focused initiatives.

She says greater access to education and employment opportunities should not be interpreted as a move away from culture or community.

It should not automatically be assumed that access equates with forgetting who we are and where we come from, or set ourselves apart from our people.

Culture is central to how many First Nations people approach their creative, academic and workplace pursuits.

Eastern Arrernte woman Tanika Anne Orr, owner of Nooks and Cooks bush food catering service, says culture has fundamentally shaped how she approaches her business.

After moving away from Country as a teenager, the now-35-year-old says forging Nooks and Cooks on Kabi Kabi Country on the Sunshine Coast became a way to reconnect with culture while building opportunities with community.

For Tanika Anne Orr, culture has also shaped the way she approaches her bush food catering business. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

"For me, it's not about being successful with money. I think for me, it's more about being successful in having that wealth around you in the way of love and connection," Orr tells SBS News.

Through her business, she hopes to share cultural knowledge and create opportunities for others.

"I really hope that my bush foods business is taking off and is employing a lot of our community."

Carrying Country wherever they go

For many young First Nations people, pursuing education, careers and leadership opportunities can involve moving between communities, cities and regions.

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, around 15 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people live in remote or very remote areas, where distance can shape access to services, education and employment opportunities.

On Gumatj Country, surrounded by the sounds and movement of Garma, young people spoke about these choices as part of their journeys — not as leaving one world behind, but as carrying who they are into new spaces.

Long, who runs Sandpoppy Weaving, moved away from home at 17 to study at QUT. While she remained relatively close to Country during her studies, she says she still felt the distance.

"Moving away as a young person definitely had its challenges, but bear in mind, I was only two hours away. I can only imagine the incredible sacrifices that many of our young people from remote and regional communities have to make," she says.

At the same time, the experience also allowed her to explore new ways First Nations stories could be shared and magnified.

It was also really amazing to see the opportunities within the metropolitan areas and the ways that our stories could be told and amplified.

Long says her decisions about education, work and future opportunities are also shaped by family and ancestors. She reflects on the significance of accessing pathways that were not available to previous generations.

"My Nana was a member of the Stolen Generation. So the fact that I can be first in family to go through to Year 10 — let alone to university and pursuing my own business — that incredible privilege is not lost on me."

A similar balancing act has shaped the journey of Willhelm Lauenstein, a Wuthathi man and Indigenous liaison officer for Royal Australian Air Force bases in Darwin and Curtin, critical northern defence facilities for the country.

While carefully painting a yidaki, a traditional Yolŋu instrument also widely known as the didgeridoo, the 32-year-old reflects on the places he has called home.

Willhelm Lauenstein says while living away from home has been challenging, connections can also be built in new places. Source: SBS News / Andrew Chappelle

After beginning his career as an electrician and later joining the Air Force, Lauenstein has lived away from his home in Cairns, including time in Katherine and Darwin.

While distance from family has been challenging, he says, connection can also be built in new places.

"I've got no family here. But now I do. Now that I've been here and [in] community and been out and amongst it all, it's like home, second home," Lauenstein tells SBS News.

For him, success also carries a sense of responsibility, especially in his role working with First Nations personnel in defence.

You need to make the right decisions. You can't really make too many wrong ones because it's not only the Elders watching you, but it's also the younger generation, they're also watching you.

Defining success on their own terms

The final pillar of success that emerged from conversations at Garma is wellbeing.

Sue-Anne Hunter, national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, says culture, language and connection to Country are central to the wellbeing and development of First Nations children and young people.

"Culture is the protective factor that keeps our children connected to their communities, to their families and to themselves," she tells SBS News.

Sue-Anne Hunter, national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, says the next generation has greater access to opportunities than ever before and is using its voice to influence the future. Source: Supplied / John Jiang

According to Hunter, young people today are accessing opportunities that were not available to many previous generations, while also using their voices to shape the future.

"What has changed is that this generation has more platforms, more opportunity and a voice they are willing to use, built on decades of advocacy by those who have come before them."

No young person should have to choose between who they are and where they are going.

Across conversations with young leaders at Gulkula, one message was clear: the future was not about choosing between where they wanted to go and where they came from — it was about carrying both forward.

title: Are you owed a share of $274 million in unclaimed money? Here's how to check
text:
In brief Services Australia says Australians are owed around $274 million in unclaimed Medicare benefits.

If you're owed, providing your bank details should allow you to receive the funds within days.

Hundreds of millions of dollars are waiting to be claimed by Australians who have not provided their current bank account details to Services Australia.

The agency says 974,000 Australians are owed a slice of $274.5 million in unpaid Medicare benefits.

It's urging people to check that their bank details are up to date in their Medicare online account.

The average amount owed per person is around $280.

Young Australians account for the largest share, with more than $65 million payable to 255,000 people aged between 18 and 24.

title: Why one tiny island's Census is about much more than numbers
text:
IN BRIEF Norfolk Island is an external territory of Australia and will take part in the Census on 11 August.

People can complete the Census online or on paper. Physical forms will be collected by field officers visiting Norfolk Island.

In the middle of the South Pacific Ocean, a tiny island spanning just 35 square kilometres will be included in this year's Census.

Home to about 2,100 residents, Norfolk Island has earned a reputation as "one of the most beautiful places on Earth", according to acting general manager of the Norfolk Island Regional Council (NIRC), Nicholas Mostardo.

He moved to the subtropical island early this year and says its natural beauty and close-knit community make it unlike anywhere else.

"It's got a rich environment, it's got very warm and kind people. It's probably one of the most unique places in the world that I've had personally the pleasure of being involved with," Mostardo told SBS News.

NIRC is currently under administration until 31 December 2026, as Norfolk Island transitions to what the Australian government has described as a "new bespoke governance model".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In the interim, Mostardo has been liaising with the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) to help ensure Norfolk Island's population is recorded during the Census of Population and Housing on 11 August.

"We've had several visits from the ABS zone manager and the assistant director of Census Mainstream and Enumeration. They've been coming out to ensure the community is well engaged and consulted on completing the form."

A decade in the making

The Census has been conducted in Australia for more than a century, but this will be the third time Norfolk Island has ever participated in the survey. It also marks a decade since the Australian government passed reforms that led to the island being included in the Census.

It's a change that was considered contentious by some.

In 1914, Norfolk became an Australian territory, but the "precise constitutional arrangement was not clear at the time", according to an online statement by legal advisory firm Norfolk Advisory.

Around 65 years later, the Australian parliament allowed Norfolk Islanders to form a limited self-government. Following governance reforms passed in 2015 and implemented in 2016, the Australian government assumed responsibility for the island's governance.

In 2023, Norfolk Island regained some involvement in its affairs through the establishment of a new advisory body, the Norfolk Island Governance Committee. The island is now considered an external territory of Australia.

This complex history has divided some people — including those of Pitcairn descent — about whether Norfolk Island should be counted during Australia's Census.

Pitcairn Islanders were a genetic mix of Tahitian and English, the English part being direct descendants from the mutineers on the HMS Bounty — a bloodline that still runs strong today. In 1856, 194 people arrived on Norfolk Island from the neighbouring Pitcairn Islands.

According to information shared with SBS News by Norfolk Island People for Democracy (NIPD), Pitcairn Islanders have a distinct culture and speak the Norf'k-Pitcairn language (also known as 'Pitkern-Norf'k' or 'Norfolk'), which blends 18th-century English and Tahitian.

NIPD has previously petitioned for the United Nations Special Committee on Decolonisation to recognise and list Norfolk Island as a non-self-governing territory. The group has described Australia's relationship with the island as a "bloodless genocide".

Norfolk Island ancestry

The ABS did not provide a statement to SBS News regarding Norfolk Island's participation in the Census. It did refer to online information available about how to complete the Census on Norfolk Island.

The ABS outlines that "ancestry data reported for Norfolk Island from the 2021 Census is not comparable with ancestry data reported from censuses prior to and including 2011". That's because of differences in the way the ancestry question was asked.

The 2011 Norfolk Island Census asked a specific question about whether a person was of Pitcairn descent. It reported that 38.4 per cent of the population identified as having Pitcairn descent.

READ MORE What is new in the 2026 Census? The questions that have changed

In Australia's 2016 Census, people could identify up to two responses when asked about their ancestry, with 29.6 per cent of usual residents indicating they had Pitcairn ancestry. During the 2021 Census, this decreased to 25.1 per cent.

The ABS notes that the number of people with Pitcairn ancestry increased from 484 in 2016 to 550 in 2021. This year, people can list up to four responses on the ancestry question.

Mostardo told SBS News that the ABS has made "some new arrangements" to provide a "better reflection of responses for people that live on Norfolk Island". He believes that has alleviated "some of the concerns that the community had [about the ancestry question] with prior censuses".

"The Census is important to Norfolk. You know, it really will assist us and the Commonwealth government with funding arrangements for the island; assisting with things like strategic planning and economic capacity as well," he said.

Norfolk Island was formed through volcanic activity in the Pacific Ocean and is located 1,676km northeast of Sydney. Credit: Peta McCartney

The Council of Elders, Norfolk Island — which serves as the elected leaders and custodians of traditional knowledge and expressions of culture on Norfolk Island — has posted content on social media regarding the Census.

In response to one Facebook user who questioned why Norfolk Island was included in the Australian Census, the group responded: "In 2016, when the ABS took over the Census, there were many shortfalls for Norfolk. The change made long-term planning for Norfolk difficult.

"As the Council of Elders' role is to advocate for the community, it became evident that we need to know more about the composition of our community today. The Council of Elders has engaged with the ABS to try to achieve this."

READ MORE Residents of a tiny Australian island are calling for a return to self-rule to save their culture

Households on Norfolk Island can complete the Census online or by using the paper form provided.

Paper forms can be returned to the Supper Room on the island during the morning from 10 August to 16 August. Otherwise, Census field officers will return to collect forms in the provided privacy envelope.

The ABS specified that forms should not be mailed back.

title: Why Australia could be heading for a spring and summer 'triple whammy'
text:
In brief Climate change, a strong El Niño and another climate driver could combine forces this spring.

However, there are signs it's not all bad news for the summer bushfire threat.

Three climate forces are lining up ahead of spring, raising the odds of hotter and drier weather across parts of Australia.

The world is facing a potentially record-breaking El Niño, with the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) forecasting it will continue to intensify into a "very strong event" that may persist well into next year.

At the same time, another Australian climate driver associated with warmer and drier conditions — a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) — is expected to develop by spring.

"So, for Australia through the coming spring and summer, the double whammy of climate change and El Niño will be driving our weather. In actual fact, we might even have a triple whammy," Andrew Watkins, an adjunct professor at Monash University and a Climate Council researcher, told SBS News.

He said the IOD "is effectively El Niño but in the Indian Ocean".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Unfortunately, that pattern really sets in until summer, when the Asian monsoon comes in and knocks it over. But if we have climate change and El Niño and a positive Indian Ocean dipole, they are three things that all push south-east Australia into hotter and drier, and especially the spring period," he said.

Will Australia see a repeat of Europe's summer?

While an El Niño does not necessarily mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia, it does raise the likelihood.

As parts of Europe and the United States swelter through a summer of scorching heatwaves and fires, BoM climatologist Zhi-Weng Chua says soon, much of Australia will likely swelter too.

He says there is a high chance much of the nation's south-east and south-west will experience one of the warmest springs on record.

"Western parts of Western Australia, extending into southern Queensland and parts of south Australia, there is a strong indication that temperatures will be in the top 20 per cent of historical records for spring," he told SBS News.

But the heat expected during Australia's spring and summer are driven by different factors to those pushing temperatures skyward in Europe and North America.

Those continents have experienced the impact of climate change in the past few months, with record-high temperatures leading to high fire danger.

READ MORE How is climate change affecting El Niño and La Niña?

El Niño is an event measured by the sea surface temperature of the Pacific Ocean — it has a strong impact on the Asia Pacific, but far less on Europe and North America.

Sea surface temperatures in the central Pacific are now more than 2C above average — a level associated with a very strong El Niño — for the first time in a decade.

Australia's bushfire outlook

Greg Mullins is the former commissioner of Fire and Rescue NSW.

In recent years, he has used his expertise to drive action on climate change preparedness and risk evaluation, as a member of the Climate Council.

He recently told SBS News this year's converging climate drivers were extremely worrying, noting that emergency agencies were working with the BoM ahead of the release of the spring bushfire seasonal outlook, which would help guide preparations.

He said the combination of an El Niño with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole could drive "flash droughts" that heighten bushfire risk.

"Those two together can drive rapid drought, what we call flash drought, that you know within weeks you're suddenly in bad fire territory," he said.

"I know there's a lot of deep concern in all the fire agencies nationally," he said.

However, BoM meteorologists said there are signs that rain could disrupt the summer bushfire threat in many areas.

"That drier than average pattern that we're seeing for September does break down for much of the country and we start seeing either above average rainfall being favoured or even a not-clear signal for a lot of the country," Chua said.

Victoria and Tasmania, however, are expected to remain comparatively dry, he said.

title: Fast-tracked for Australian citizenship, this sports star has her sights set on LA 2028
text:
In brief Para taekwondo athlete Shrijana Ghising hopes to represent Australia at the 2028 Paralympics.

She was granted fast-tracked citizenship by the federal government.

Shrijana Ghising took up para taekwondo for fun when she was 18.

Eight years later, the 26-year-old is one of the world's top athletes in the sport and is chasing a place at the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles.

And as one of Australia's newest citizens, she hopes she will be wearing green and gold.

Originally from Nepal, Ghising won silver at the Gangwon-Chuncheon 2026 World Para Taekwondo Open Challenge in South Korea earlier this month — her first international tournament representing Australia.

"I'm so excited that now I am a citizen I can represent Australia in all the tournaments, but the big goal is LA28 … I want to be a medallist representing Australia," she said.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

She travelled to Australia on holiday in 2023 but quickly fell in love with the country.

"I have experienced a lot of discrimination in my life, but when I came to Australia everyone was very kind, and they did not treat me differently because of my disability," she said.

"Everyone in Australia is treated with the same respect.

Ghising won silver at the Gangwon-Chuncheon 2026 World Para Taekwondo Open Challenge in South Korea. Source: Supplied

"I love Australia, its culture and its people … I came for a holiday, but it became my home."

Ghising lived in Burnie, Tasmania, for two years before moving to Melbourne to further pursue her taekwondo career.

"My mother and my life partner motivated me to fulfil my taekwondo journey," she said.

Under special provisions of the Citizenship Act and with authorisation from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Ghising's citizenship application was expedited so she could compete for Australia at upcoming tournaments.

She officially became an Australian citizen at a ceremony in Melbourne's inner-west in June — just in time to represent Australia at the Para Taekwondo Open Challenge.

Australia has a special citizenship pathway for elite athletes and coaches to represent the country internationally.

The law was changed last year so Australian permanent residents who train or compete overseas as part of their sporting commitments are not disadvantaged in their pathway to citizenship, a move welcomed by the Australian Olympic Committee and Paralympics Australia.

However, refugee advocacy groups have previously said the rules should be broadened to include all people applying for Australian citizenship.

In 2009, when the government proposed shortening residency requirements for elite athletes, the Federation of Ethnic Communities' Councils of Australia welcomed the change but said it wanted everybody to be treated equally under citizenship law.

In 2024-25, a total of 165,193 people became Australian citizens, representing over 190 different nationalities.

Damien Kilner, from the Department of Home Affairs, said the federal government worked closely with sporting bodies to identify citizenship pathways for athletes seeking to represent Australia.

"Shrijana's journey from being a visitor who fell in love with this country to now preparing to represent the green and gold on the world stage highlights the important contributions new citizens can make to Australia and our international success," he said.

Ghising picked up para taekwondo for fun when she was a teenager. Source: Supplied

Paralympics Australia chief executive Cameron Murray welcomed Ghising to the Australian Paralympic movement.

"Para sport offers so much to Australians with disability, and it is pleasing that Shrijana is already experiencing its value, which can extend far beyond sport," he said.

"As part of our lead role within the Australian sporting system, Paralympics Australia looks forward to working with our partners to support Shrijana's journey as she strives to represent Australia on the international stage.

"Her story exemplifies the values that make our Paralympic movement so special: courage, resilience and the pursuit of opportunity."

title: What the upcoming nationwide e-bike crackdown means for you
text:
In brief New rules are set to come into place governing the use and capabilities of e-bikes.

The ACCC is drafting the new rules, which the government hopes will address safety issues.

A nationwide crackdown on high-speed e-bikes will seek to close regulatory loopholes after years of rising accidents and injuries, the federal government has announced.

On Thursday, Labor instructed the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to draft new standards for the sale of "e-micromobility" devices.

The new standards will apply to electric bikes, scooters and skateboards and are designed to prevent the sale of high-risk devices following a spike in e-bike injuries.

Assistant Competition Minister Andrew Leigh said the changes would inspire confidence in Australian consumers and send a clear message to industry.

"Nationally consistent standards will provide clearer expectations for manufacturers, retailers and consumers alike," he said.

What rules are currently in place for e-bikes?

Currently, regulatory enforcement varies between states and territories. Retailers can exploit the resultant loopholes to sell non-compliant devices.

Last year, Australia's state transport ministers agreed to mandate the international EN 15194 standard as the primary benchmark for e-bikes.

These standards restrict e-bikes to operating primarily through pedal assistance, cap their output, and require them to cut power once they reach 25km/h.

The new rules drafted by the ACCC will aim to close existing gaps after years of concerns over injuries and accidents, including from high-powered e-bikes.

The new consumer standards were proposed at a meeting of federal, state and territory consumer affairs ministers in Darwin in July.

Are the rules likely to be effective?

Harold Scruby, chief executive at the Pedestrian Council of Australia, said the announcement was a welcome step forward, but long overdue.

"It is too late," he told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

"Technology is always 10 years ahead of the law ... (but) we saw it coming."

Any changes must be complemented by consequences for retailers who fail to meet compliance standards, Scruby said.

Shared e-bike schemes have created a number of problems in many cities, but are used by many residents. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

"We've really got to clamp down on these cowboys who are selling these things to young children," he said.

Asked whether the horse had already bolted, Leigh insisted the changes complemented state-level crackdowns.

"There's work underway through transport ministers," he told Seven's Sunrise program on Thursday.

"This is about what can be sold."

Why are e-bikes so controversial?

E-bikes have been spruiked as an environmentally friendly, cost-affordable answer to congested city streets.

But the rollout of shared e-bike schemes — like Lime bikes and others — as well as their broader uptake across the nation have been clouded by rising injury and accident rates.

In 2024, NSW recorded 226 injuries related to e-bikes, which surged to 233 in the first seven months of 2025, including four deaths.

In Queensland, more than 6000 emergency department presentations were linked to e‑mobility devices between 2022 and 2025.

READ MORE Faulty e-bike battery sparks Sydney apartment evacuation

Queensland is among the states cracking down on illegal e-bikes, including with its police force's Operation Yankee Surety.

Some 249 illegal bikes were seized in the operation's first month following its launch on July 1, while riders were hit with 991 traffic infringement notices.

NSW Police and transport officers were in June granted powers to seize illegal e-bikes, to be pulverised by Transport for NSW.

Both states have been undertaking sweeping reforms of the electronic transport devices, but measures announced today will be the first nationwide effort to reform their use.

When will the new rules come into effect?

Work on the ACCC new e-micromobility standard is already underway.

Further details on enforcement timelines are unlikely to be released until consultation can be carried out with industry bodies and state regulators.

title: 'Don't bank on it': Three factors shaping next week's interest rates decision
text:
in brief The Reserve Bank board will decide on Tuesday whether to leave the cash rate at 4.35 per cent or change it.

Inflation, unemployment and household spending are three key economic indicators shaping the decision.

Millions of borrowers will be watching closely when the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) announces its latest interest rates decision next week.

A mortgage expert says it will be a close call despite expectations among the 'big four' banks — Commonwealth Bank, Westpac, NAB and ANZ — that the central bank will leave the cash rate on hold at 4.35 per cent.

The RBA has already lifted rates three times this year, while governor Michele Bullock has refused to rule out further hikes as inflation remains above its 2-3 per cent target band.

"They've got a clock ticking in the background, particularly when it comes to inflation," said Sally Tindall, the data insights director at Canstar.

"The RBA board has repeatedly said that time is a factor in this battle with inflation because the longer we take to get back down, the harder it becomes, and the more entrenched inflation becomes".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The board will examine three key economic indicators released in recent weeks before handing down its decision on Tuesday.

Inflationary pressures

Inflationary pressures, as measured by both the consumer price index (CPI) and trimmed mean inflation, are frequently cited in the RBA's statements on its decision-making.

In June, the RBA said inflation was still too high and warned higher fuel and commodity costs are starting to flow into other parts of the economy, including housing and construction.

Bullock said Australia already had an inflation problem before disruptions to global oil markets caused by conflict in the Middle East.

The most recent data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) showed a shift in inflation in June.

Headline inflation fell from 4 per cent to 3.8 per cent while the trimmed mean, which strips out volatile items, remained steady at 3.6 per cent.

Source: SBS News

Tindall said that inflation predictions have shifted over time primarily due to the war in the Middle East, which has added to inflationary pressures.

The figures for June were "perhaps better than we were expecting," Tindall said, "but still a long way from target".

Source: SBS News

The RBA aims to bring inflation down to between 2 and 3 per cent, fulfilling one of its mandates to keep it low and stable.

Its other mandate is to support full employment, meaning as many Australians in work as possible without creating excessive inflation.

Unemployment rate

Tindall described the unemployment rate as "a critical data set for the RBA".

In June, the unemployment rate was 4.4 per cent, slightly below the 2026 peak of 4.5 per cent in April.

Source: SBS News

These figures have been on the RBA governor's mind. Earlier this month, Bullock said they were higher than expected.

However, Tindall said that while elevated, this figure of 4.4 per cent in itself is not going to push the board into "ringing an alarm bell".

Consumer spending

The amount households spend can give a sense of the average Australian's disposable income after they've made their mortgage payments.

This indicator gives the RBA a window into how households are faring amid economic pressures, including cost of living and the impact of higher interest rates.

READ MORE Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold

However, Tindall said this data can be hard to interpret.

"It's difficult to isolate in this data the families that are doing it incredibly tough versus the ones that aren't really sweating from the economic pressures at the moment," she said.

In June 2026, household spending rose 0.8 per cent month-on-month.

"Going further back with this data set, it's actually quite volatile, and there have been rises in June and May but a fall in April," Tindall said.

"The RBA will be paying attention to this, but will also look at other data points, including liaison programs, to better understand how Australian families are going."

Source: SBS News

Under these liaison programs, RBA economists consult with hundreds of private firms, industry associations, government agencies, and community organisations across Australia.

'Don't bank on it'

While the big four banks expect the RBA to leave rates unchanged on Tuesday, Tindall said borrowers should still be prepared for the possibility of another rate rise.

"I would say if you've got a mortgage, don't bank on it. Spend the weekend just going over your finances, making sure that you can withstand another rate hike. It might not happen on Tuesday, but it could still happen in the future," she said.

The big four banks predict the RBA won't move on rates until next year, when it will likely make its first cut since August 2025.

But that could change should overseas conflict escalate and put pressure on essential products like oil.

"Go out there and see if you can potentially get yourself a better deal with your bank," Tindall said.

"You can use the interest rate uncertainty as ammunition to negotiate with your own bank, or you could end up ultimately refinancing.

"But if you can get your own personalised rate cut, that will help future-proof your finances should we see another rate hike."

title: ‘A torpedo’: Italy-Spain border blow-up now a major headache for Europe – and Australian travellers
text:
Advertisement

Analysis WorldEuropeRefugees ‘A torpedo’: Italy-Spain border blow-up now a major headache for Europe – and Australian travellers David Crowe August 8, 2026 — 11:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: A sudden move has deepened a border dispute between Spain and Italy that could delay thousands of travellers moving between the countries – and erode a pivotal agreement on passport checks across Europe. Spain has called on Italy to lift border controls that it imposed last week following a rush of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Migrants returning to Morocco from the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in late July. AP Italy has refused to relent after being given a Sunday deadline to drop its additional controls, and Spain has retaliated with measures of its own. The result is the rapid imposition of passport checks on many travellers moving directly between the two countries – something not seen in decades.

Advertisement

Tempers are running hot. Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares described the Italian border policy as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”. Speaking on Friday in Europe (Friday night, AEST), he said that Madrid was prepared to respond with a tough approach of its own. Hours later, it did just that. This is now a major headache for the European Union. And travellers from Australia. Italy has suspended the usual rules for travellers from outside the European Union who arrive from Spain, declaring that it needs the stronger safeguards until at least August 15. Spain has decided to do the same for those who arrive from Italy. This applies from midnight on Saturday – 8am on Sunday, AEST – at Spanish borders. So, officials will conduct passport, nationality and visa checks for Italian passengers and visitors from other countries arriving from Italy.

Advertisement

Australians travelling between the two countries will need to be on guard for additional controls. What began as a diplomatic dispute about Ceuta is turning into a test of the Schengen Agreement that was signed in 1985 to waive passport checks on travellers moving across the internal borders of most EU member states. Loading At its best, the Schengen Agreement allows the citizens of 29 member countries to move easily across their borders without a passport check, visa or electronic travel authority. For visitors from Australia and other countries, it also ensures relatively seamless travel across those internal EU borders. Once the traveller arrives at the first Schengen member state and clears passport control, there is usually no need for any other passport check when moving to other member states inside the Schengen zone.

Advertisement

This has been so successful that the initial agreement of 1985 was codified in a convention in 1990 and extended many times to the point where the Schengen zone now has a population of 450 million people. The latest expansion came last year when Romania and Bulgaria joined in full. Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right For Australians on longer journeys, the only challenge with the Schengen zone is making sure they don’t visit for more than 90 days in any 180-day period – the basic rule that often leads to side-trips to non-Schengen states such as Britain or Ireland. (While Ireland is in the EU, it never joined Schengen.) But now, Schengen is under some strain. The argument between Italy and Spain comes amid other tensions at European borders. The new digital Entry/Exit System, or EES, has led to long queues at passport control for non-EU nationals, who must be registered with the new system.

Advertisement

Travellers have missed flights because of sluggish checks at border control kiosks, where officials gather fingerprints and photographs to enter each person into the vast new database. It is an operational failure. The workaround at some airports is to halt the EES for a period and return to old ways of clearing queues. A 12-year-old who crossed into Spain is escorted by a Spanish soldier to the Spain-Morocco border this week, as the child begs not to be sent back to Morocco. AP The new argument about Schengen, however, is foundational. It is about whether Schengen has become a point of weakness for Europe when so many are concerned about illegal arrivals and asylum seekers. Political leaders are responding to clear signals that voters want lower migration. Spain insists that the concern is overblown. Its latest estimate is that 72,000 people entered Ceuta from Morocco in the final days of July. It says almost all of them returned to Morocco. Crucially, Ceuta is not in the Schengen zone. Adult migrants who get to Ceuta have to clear other checks before they can reach the European mainland.

Advertisement

Thousands of the migrants are still in Ceuta, though. Spanish authorities have confirmed about 1100 unaccompanied minors are still in the enclave and have a legal right to remain. They are likely to be transferred to Spain. Related Article Aviation ‘Bring food and water’: Australians face six-hour lines for Euro summer Even so, Italy will not drop its concern about illegal migrants getting to Spain and taking advantage of easy travel across borders into Italy. So Spain has chosen to retaliate. In practical terms, this means Italian officials check passports for non-EU citizens arriving from Spain. Since there is no land border between the two, it entails checks on flights from Madrid, Barcelona, ​​Ibiza, Valencia and other Spanish locations, as well as some ferries. Italy appears to have an agreement with France to have stronger checks on land border crossings, but it is not clear what difference this makes.

Advertisement

The Spanish response appears likely to mean additional checks on all travellers arriving directly from Italian airports. Related Article Immigration ‘I don’t know why they let us through’: How 50,000 people surged into a Spanish exclave Travellers moving through other Schengen states should not see any change – not for now, at least. But everything depends on whether the argument between Italy and Spain spreads to their neighbours. What if other countries decide they too want to erect barriers against arrivals from Spain because of the anxiety about migrants in Ceuta? As right-wing leaders in Europe demand bigger and stronger borders, it will be tempting for governments to toughen their policies, even if Spain insists that it has the problem under control.

Advertisement

For the moment, Italy and Spain are set to intensify their fight over national pride and border policy by making queues longer at their airports. And by punishing travellers. title: The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass
text:
Advertisement

Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The new Wallabies coach has copped an early hospital pass Paul Cully August 8, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Les Kiss’ first Test as Wallabies coach could easily turn into the shocker in Osaka. The heat and humidity they are likely to encounter is one factor, but aside from that, Japan are a competitive Test side underpinned by an improving domestic competition filled with high-quality coaches from around the world. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Les Kiss chat at training ahead of Saturday’s match against Japan. Getty Images The Brave Blossoms were messed around by Ireland’s recent refusal to travel to Japan in the Nations Championship, but they have won the scheduling battle for this two-Test series against the Wallabies. Kiss would have copped the odd hospital pass as a player. Now, as a coach, he’s got a high ball well above his shoulders with Eddie Jones steaming in from 20 metres away.

Advertisement

The Wallabies could lose this Test. The bar for success in Kiss’ debut as coach is a win of any nature: get the job done and get out of there. It is a Test with a high-risk profile, and Kiss was never going to be able to fully mitigate that risk, no matter how he selected his team. Loading However, his 23-man squad and the make-up of the bench have increased the likelihood of Japan getting away to the fast start they desperately want. Josh Canham and Miles Amatosero are a young pairing, and they will face Warner Dearns, the best second-rower in Super Rugby Pacific this season, while prop Aidan Ross is more solid than spectacular and certainly won’t offer the same mobility around the field as Angus Bell.

Advertisement

Jones has prioritised speed from the outset, preferring Jack Cornelsen in the second row ahead of Harry Hockings, and Amatosero is going to be tested by the speed of the game if Japan get the quick ball they want. Clearly, the Wallabies’ strategy is to finish the Test strongly with their stacked bench, but they won’t want to be chasing the game with the combative Hockings and that old warrior Michael Leitch providing serious nuisance value off the bench for Jones. Eddie Jones and Japan will be ready for the challenge posed by the Wallabies. Getty Images The Wallabies must have considered the opposite approach – trying to overwhelm the Japanese early. That is something the French did well in June. Japan probably don’t even know themselves what a good side they are, but their self-belief will soar if they start well and exert scoreboard pressure on the Wallabies.

Advertisement

A Japan XV side put themselves in a great position against the Maori All Blacks in late June, racing into a 24-7 lead at halftime during their game in Nagoya, before that lack of self-belief kicked in. They were chased down and lost 38-31. But they will have learnt something from that defeat and young No.10 Ryunosuke Ito probably banked some valuable lessons as he continues his crash-course introduction to Test rugby. Loading The other player to look for is Japan No.6 Ben Gunter, who is on a big collision course with Wallaby Rob Valetini. Gunter, who grew up in Australia, has arguably the biggest shoulders in Test rugby and is not afraid to use them. He has snuck under the radar this week with all the focus on Hockings, but Gunter is the better player. He is an old-fashioned hitman who will also be lining up Harry Wilson if the Wallabies captain comes off the back fence.

Advertisement

The Jones factor is also inescapable, and the former Wallabies coach will have some clear views on how and where Kiss’s side can be vulnerable. Related Article Australian rugby Hoop dreams: How growing up on a court turned Josh into a Wallabies ‘baller’ But it’s a factor that is easy to overplay in a rugby world in which the degrees of separation between Australian rugby and Japan are decreasing anyway. For example, new Wallabies defence coach Scott McLeod almost won the Japan Rugby League One title in June (against Dave Rennie’s Kobe) as an assistant at Kubota Spears. In a classic clash of styles, Kubota employed a kicking and defence-based game plan, using the tactical nous of new/old Waratahs No.10 Bernard Foley.

Advertisement

Against Rennie’s ball-in-hand style – and Kobe superstar Ardie Savea – it almost worked too: Kubota might have won the game but for a knock-on by former Crusaders halfback Bryn Hall with the tryline in sight. That decider was a good showcase for the tactical variety and physicality of the Japanese game, and their players are increasingly well-prepared for the demands of Test rugby. Kiss, therefore, has been handed a tricky first assignment – and if he marks it with a victory, it is a bigger positive than he will get credit for. title: My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss
text:
Advertisement

NationalGen Z Opinion My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss Julia Baird Journalist, broadcaster, historian and author August 8, 2026 — 9:30am

August 8, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I can’t believe,” says my daughter as I navigate our rented manual car around the narrow, cobbled streets of Nazaré, Portugal, “that you used to have to read maps to travel.” As the gears grind yet again under my rusty touch, I glance at her and laugh: “But we were using a whole part of our brain that you guys don’t touch now.” She shrugs, tapping on her phone. Illustration by Dionne Gain Remember maps? Calling from a phone box? Aerogram letters? Post-school travel for those born in the ’70s meant disappearing into Europe like a gumboot into quicksand, swallowed whole by different cultures. We were not being monitored, surveilled, tracked: we were finding our own paths, new ones. We didn’t have mobile phones with location data, downloadable maps, apps to make bookings. This, too, confounds my daughter: “But your parents wouldn’t know if you were dead.” I guess they just waved us off and hoped for the best. There was something delightful about the invisibility, being out of range and absolved of all responsibility. We were just gone, and we’d be back in a few months. Sure, I’d call home every week or two – collect, to the eye-rolls of my parents – and send the odd postcard, but that was it. We took photos on little cameras and mailed the film back home to be developed: they were unfailingly blurry, unflattering, often tilted or poorly framed. But it wasn’t about how we looked, it was about what we were looking at. There are few things as genuinely thrilling about entering and inhaling a new country for the first time. We took terrible risks, sleeping on beaches, train stations, boat shacks, all to save money, and relied on overnight train trips to get some rest, zigzagging around the continent with a heavily stamped Eurail Pass.

Advertisement

My daughter and her friends are too smart to do stupid things like sleep in public places. But I watch the reels and feeds of this Euro-generation, who save up and go year after year to the prettiest places in Europe, navigating swelling crowds, and I am gobsmacked. Julia Baird in Venice during her own backpacker adventure. First, they look so good. Polished and picture-perfect. I think I packed a hairbrush, but I can’t be sure. Maybe an eyeliner? Nothing more. I was gripped by an Oscar Wilde biography (the superb work by Richard Ellmann) and was somehow inspired by that to invest in several vintage Spanish brocade jackets which were hopeless in the cold and probably looked half mad, paired with scuffed Doc Martens and cut-off jeans. Today I scroll through Instagram and see a string of girls in bikinis and impeccable, tasteful clothes. Carousels of cute poses. Second, there is an ease to travel we did not know, facilitated by the phone and by the now-widespread fluency in English across Europe. If we didn’t make an effort to learn the local language, we were cooked: Google Translate didn’t exist. According to travel research group MMGY’s 2025 Portrait of European Travellers (surveying France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK), Gen Z (aged 14-29) is responsible for the travel boom in Europe, and is planning to spend more on global travel and take more vacations than any other age bracket. Unsurprisingly, Italy, Spain and Greece are considered the most desirable, while the US flags in popularity. They are using planning tools and AI to map out itineraries.

Advertisement

But tech isn’t just aiding travel, it’s shaping and changing it. The most picturesque, Insta-worthy places are swamped by young people looking for the perfect shot to post, much to the annoyance of locals. Sweating crowds in sweltering Europe jostle around landmarks and crowd the most photogenic vistas. Today in the centre of Lisbon, where I have come to research a book, on the way to the train station I wove past dozens of people in Instagram poses, hands on hips, laughing, tilting heads, pouting, flexing. What they are missing is the joy of not being seen. Of waking up on beaches with panda eyes, not worrying someone will take a shot and post it. I remember speaking a year ago to one teen who was preparing for a Mediterranean trip by having her eyelashes, nails and brows done: “No way am I going to be chopped [look unattractive] in Greece,” she said. The prevalence of social media has also led to milder behaviour, according to a 2024 survey by youth travel agency StudentUniverse. It found only one in five young Australians planned to party when travelling overseas: 84 per cent of Gen Z full-time students scheduled trips where there would be no drinking. Many parents would cheer, given the genuine concerns about drink-spiking and safety, but 27 per cent of Gen Z also said they just didn’t want to be snapped doing something embarrassing.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Tourism Idiots are ruining travel for the rest of us Ben Groundwater Travel writer StudentUniverse’s Will Jones told Student Traveller this trend – of “dry-trippers” – had been rapid and widespread: “This is the first generation to be setting this trend. I’m a Millennial and I remember when I was their age having holidays focused on drinking and partying. So it is amazing how much, and how quickly, this has changed. “Australians used to be seen as big party people, but this Gen Z is the first global generation. Because of social media, they all seem to be following the same trends and doing the same things.” This is a generation that is having less sex, drinking less and reading fewer books (although they are reading in digital formats). But they are travelling more often. War or global instability haven’t deterred them, with only 1.5 per cent of Australians under 30 cancelling trips to Europe in 2026. Home ownership is hard, almost impossible; holidays are within reach.

Advertisement

In 2023, The Guardian declared “gritty gap years” were out and “grand tours of Europe’s charisma” were in. Is it weird to be nostalgic about the grit? A time when we could run wild, unobserved, learning how to fend for ourselves? When we could just have fun – or not – instead of feeling like we also had to look like we were having fun? I realise this makes me seem ancient. I also feel like I’m describing the daily life of ancient explorers. But in trading concealment for convenience, evaporation for ease, surely we are in danger of losing the pleasure of forgetting ourselves and truly paying attention, marvelling. Julia Baird is a journalist, author and regular columnist. Her latest book is Bright Shining: How grace changes everything.
